articles.title_orig: Election Dispatches: Talarico Remains Ahead in Texas Senate Race, Polls Show, but His Lead Has Narrowed
articles.title_zh: Election Dispatches: Talarico Remains Ahead in Texas Senate Race, Polls Show, but His Lead Has Narrowed
articles.content_orig:
Talarico casts himself as a moderate who would put Texans’ needs over party allegiances amid close contest against Republican Ken Paxton
James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, sat face to face with several undecided voters who grilled him on a slew of contentious issues including Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, abortion and foreign aid, during a CNN town hall on Wednesday evening.
One voter, a devout small business owner, questioned the authenticity of Talarico’s faith, referencing a past remark where he described God as nonbinary.
“When I said that, I was being provocative and I want to admit that and come clean about that,” Talarico responded. “What I was saying is actually not controversial theologically: the idea that we can’t define God using human categories. Not only did I say that, but the late Charlie Kirk said that – the late Pope Benedict said that.”
Talarico added that he was receptive to feedback from Christians.
Jodi Hunt, a self-described single-issue voter, probed Talarico’s pro-choice stance, asking: “How would you convince me as a Catholic voter that I can trust you would protect the most innocent among us?”
Talarico described the Bible as being silent on abortion, to which Hunt countered quoting “Thou shalt not kill”.
“We may have different, moral conclusions when it comes to this particular ethical question, but we actually have the same public policy goal,” Talarico said, framing abortion as a public health issue that could be solved with a reduction in unplanned pregnancies.
During the night, Talarico cast himself as a moderate, who would put the needs of Texans over party allegiances. He railed against the ultra-wealthy, framing them as the common enemy.
Talarico and the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton , are locked in a competitive race to become Texas’s next US senator, with most recent polls showing Talarico with a narrow lead over Paxton. (Paxton declined an invitation to appear on CNN, host Erin Burnett said at the start of the town hall.)
Though Democrats have not won a Senate seat in the state since the late 1980s, they’re hoping Talarico’s newcomer energy and popular appeal will persuade independents and Republicans fed up with Donald Trump’s second term – or turned off by Paxton’s many scandals.
Over the weekend, Talarico became the subject of a disinformation campaign after he was absent from the campaign trail for more than a week. While Talarico’s campaign repeatedly said the candidate was sick with a bad case of the flu, conservative influencers falsely accused him of receiving medical treatment at a mental health facility in Ohio.
The rumor was further propelled by Paxton and Trump, who sought to fuel skepticism about Talarico’s health and fitness for office.
The Democratic candidate denied the false allegations after returning to the campaign trail last week, noting he had never been to Ohio.
“False claims got millions of views online and this is an example of what I call the ‘rage economy’,” Talarico said during the town hall. “Billionaires who own these platforms get rich. We all get angry and nobody’s life gets any better. Conspiracy theories don’t put food on the table, put gas in the tank, or improve our communities.”
Paxton, meanwhile, has been battling his own controversies. A series of leaked audio recordings – made during a closed-door meeting – have been posted online and revealed him being critical of his own party and campaign leaders in DC .
Paxton entered the race with a history of scandals. He was impeached by the Texas state legislature in 2023 on allegations including bribery and abuse of public trust, though he was later acquitted. Paxton’s wife of almost four decades, Angela Paxton, then filed for divorce in 2025 on “biblical grounds”, citing adultery.
But Trump endorsed Paxton to run against Talarico, passing up incumbent Republican John Cornyn.

articles.title_orig: Iranian attacks sink two ships in Strait of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Iranian attacks sink two ships in Strait of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
Two cargo ships have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being struck by unknown projectiles in separate incidents – highlighting the heightened danger to shipping as Iran steps up attacks in an attempt to regain control over the critical waterway.
The Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pride was struck on Tuesday while passing through the strait, catching fire and later sinking, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. All crew members were safely evacuated.
Videos verified by CNN show black smoke rising from the ship as it takes on water, while later footage and satellite images show cargo scattered in the water and a small oil slick. Iranian state media Press TV reported that the ship had “hit a sea mine on an unauthorized route” – which experts cast doubt on, saying a drone attack was more likely.
The merchant vessel Cape Dao, registered under Antigua and Barbuda, also sank, according to data from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) on Wednesday – after it was first hit by projectile on September 23. One Indian crew member was killed.
While many vessels have been hit in the Strait of Hormuz this year, these are only the second and third to have sunk in the Middle East since the Iran war began in February, according to IMO data. Attacks have ramped up significantly since the end of September, once again reducing the amount of oil transiting out of the Middle East and raising oil prices around the world.
That’s been a consistent headache for US President Donald Trump as the midterm elections approach, with gas prices, tariffs, and other factors driving up the cost of living top of mind for many voters.
Data from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) , which monitors shipping incidents, shows just how high the risk is. Nine attacks in or near the Strait of Hormuz have been reported since Monday, including a drone strike on a tanker.
Only 4.147 million barrels of oil successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz on Monday – less than a quarter of pre-war levels, according to maritime data tracking service Kpler. And the seven-day average of oil flow through Hormuz has dropped sharply since early October, Kpler’s data shows.
“The sinking of Singapore-flagged GFS PRIDE marks a dangerous escalation after weeks of near-daily attacks on commercial shipping. Iran claims a naval mine; but a drone strike is more likely,” said former US Navy officer Charlie Brown, also a senior adviser for United Against Nuclear Iran, a nonprofit that tracks and reports on Iranian sanctions violations.
“Many ask what response will the US Navy mount to Iran’s escalating attacks on global shipping,” he added. “But the real question is what response will other nations take? How long will the world tolerate this threat to shipping, seafarers and freedom of navigation?”
After oil increasingly left the Gulf, Iran is trying to regain its stranglehold on shipping
The US military continues to enforce a blockade on Iranian ports to maintain economic pressure on Iran. To some extent, it’s worked: Iran’s economy is in tatters, and in recent months it clearly lost its leverage over the strait, with the amount of oil flowing from other Gulf nations through the waterway increasing to near-normal levels .
That’s partly thanks to a complex operation involving US-military-escorted “dark” transits across the strait at night, with tankers turning off their transponders to avoid detection.
That rise in oil flow is why Iran is now ramping up its attacks and threats, hoping to wrestle back the leverage it once had over the strait – especially as American voters head to the polls.
The Trump administration has tried to lower prices in other ways, including a controversial deal announced last week to drop some sanctions on Russia to import a relatively small amount of the country’s diesel. But this has been met with bipartisan criticism – and there’s no guarantee it will bring any substantial relief, with analysts warning that diesel could climb near all-time highs by November.
CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: White House defends new press secretary amid questions about her legal credentials
articles.title_zh: White House defends new press secretary amid questions about her legal credentials
articles.content_orig:
The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.
President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week and she has referred to herself as a lawyer.
But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China."
She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".
Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."
On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.
They are seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".
The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.
A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US.
The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself.
She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.
Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.
A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.
She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.
Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.
In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.
In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.
The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment.
It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work.
Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.

articles.title_orig: Ancient Chinese parents gave babies nicknames – ‘Dog’, ‘Pig’ – to protect them
articles.title_zh: Ancient Chinese parents gave babies nicknames – ‘Dog’, ‘Pig’ – to protect them
articles.content_orig:
Some believe these humble nicknames carry parents’ heartfelt blessings and should be preserved
Like people elsewhere in the world, Chinese people often have nicknames in addition to their official names. Some of these may surprise people from other cultures because they sound humble or even unflattering.
Chinese parents have traditionally given their children humble, sometimes vulgar, nicknames – occasionally using animal names such as “Dog” or “Pig.” The practice dates back to ancient times.
Parents believed that the humbler a nickname sounded, the better, as it might help ensure their child grew up healthy.
This practice was a desperate measure in ancient times, when medical technology was limited and people’s average lifespans were short.

articles.title_orig: U.S. warnings sow confusion, alarm in Ukraine over intelligence, Starlink access
articles.title_zh: U.S. warnings sow confusion, alarm in Ukraine over intelligence, Starlink access
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said Wednesday that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump was responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network.
Writing on X, Musk said that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Ukraine had accused SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on the Starshield internet service without warning, leading to disruptions to Ukrainian military operations amid fresh Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
On Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said SpaceX had implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion, without notifying the country's defense forces.
That had disrupted some missions, and the same restrictions also applied to Starshield, he said on Telegram . Starlink is used to operate Ukraine's interceptor drones, the "most effective solution" against Moscow's Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said.
Starshield is a military-grade satellite network, while Starlink is only meant for "civilian or defensive activities," Musk said.
Some restrictions appear to have been partially lifted, with former Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov thanking Musk early Thursday morning that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers an hour had been restored. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," Fedorov added.
The developments come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over an "energy ceasefire," between Ukraine and Russia announced by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukraine has, however, welcomed a deal subject to Moscow honoring its commitment, while Russian authorities said talks were ongoing, without confirming whether they had reached an agreement. On Monday, Zelenskyy accused the Russians of breaching the ceasefire.
Trump had also taken aim at Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities, saying that Kyiv's attacks were responsible for the increase in diesel prices, instead of the U.S.' war with Iran.
Washington has threatened to cut intelligence sharing with Kyiv, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Ukrainian officials said a day earlier that they have not received warnings of Russian attacks on the country for two straight days.
— CNBC's Elsa Olhen contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI Engineer, Who Is Charged With Planting Bug, Advised Saudis
articles.title_zh: OpenAI Engineer, Who Is Charged With Planting Bug, Advised Saudis
articles.content_orig:
The Saudi national accused of bugging OpenAI’s headquarters booked a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia before his arrest, US prosecutors have alleged.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, had been scheduled to fly to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member on October 12, prosecutors said in a court filing unsealed on Wednesday.
The FBI arrested Alfozan, who worked at OpenAI for about 15 months until his termination last week, on October 9, after OpenAI personnel reported the discovery of a hidden listening device in a conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters.
Alfozan, 35, has been charged with “using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications”.
The offence carries a maximum punishment of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
Prosecutors disclosed the alleged flight booking to a judge on October 8 in a motion seeking to seal the criminal complaint against Alfozan, arguing he had the “means – and will have an incentive – to flee” the United States.
William Pernik, Alfozan’s lawyer, said he and his client planned to contest the criminal allegations and his client’s ongoing detention in court.
“We trust that the American justice system will treat our client fairly, despite the narrative painted in the media at this time,” Pernik told Al Jazeera.
“Our client is a well regarded professional with long standing ties to the community,” Pernik added.
“He is presumed innocent and is entitled to fair treatment and due process of law. The emphasis on his national origin and therefore suggestions of lack of trustworthiness or flight risk harken back to dark chapters of our nation’s history that we intend to fight fully.”
Alfozan’s arrest has shone a spotlight on concerns that frontier tech firms are a target for spying and industrial espionage amid the global race to gain an upper hand in AI.
Before joining OpenAI in July last year, Alfozan worked as a systems engineer at Meta and interned at Microsoft, according to a LinkedIn profile in his name.
Alfozan is also listed as a venture partner at Raed Ventures, a Riyadh-based venture capital firm whose other partners include Prince Khalid bin Bandar bin Sultan bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family.
In a statement announcing Alfozan’s appointment in February 2025, Raed Ventures described the engineer as “a seasoned professional with extensive experience in tech startups” and said his role would involve “identifying promising investment opportunities and supporting startups on their journey toward growth and success”.

articles.title_orig: Hastings Introduces Regional Demonstrators Program
articles.title_zh: Hastings Introduces Regional Demonstrators Program
articles.content_orig:
Hastings Fiber Glass Products has expanded its Demonstrator program and introduced regional Demonstrators to provide better, dedicated coverage of the United States hot line tools and equipment market.
By adding three new Demonstrators and subject matter experts to its team, the program staff now possesses a combined 95 years of field experience using hot line tools and equipment.
In addition to long-time Hastings ’ team member John Giancanelli, the Demonstrator team now includes Ben Hoover, Colby Quaife and Ryon Roberts.
As a Demonstrator, each team member uses first-hand industry knowledge to show proper tool use and capabilities, provide safety and compliance instruction, manage client relationships and relay feedback to engineering for product innovation and improvements.
“Expanding our Demonstrator presence with people who know the job and the tools is important for Hastings Fiber Glass Products,” said Brian Baum, CEO of Hastings . “Having people who have worked in the field, know the risks first-hand and can share practical, real-world solutions helps keep end users of Hastings ’ products safe and supported on the job.
“John has been the foundation of our educational efforts for nearly two decades,” Baum said. “Adding Ben, Colby, and Ryon to the team will help expand upon his expertise and coverage area.”
Before joining Hastings in 2008, Giancanelli worked as a lineworker, first responder, and lead in the field for 20 years. He relocated from Hastings ’ headquarters in Michigan to Texas, allowing him to focus on the central United States, including North Dakota and Minnesota, south to Texas. He shares Arkansas and Louisiana with Quaife and Roberts, and Wyoming, Colorado and New Mexico with Hoover.
“I’ve restored power due to earthquakes, riots, fires, floods, avalanches and various storms,” Giancanelli said. “I can’t think of much I didn’t do in line work from 115 kV down, and I’m thankful for the experience.”
In his role at Hastings , he enjoys having face-to-face conversations and being able to provide answers and solutions in real time.
“The customers know we’ve traveled to see them, which is important, especially if they have a problem,” he added. “Listening to them and then providing a qualified, satisfying solution is rewarding.”
As a new addition to the team, Hoover, who is based in Colorado, covers the West Coast and eastward as far as Montana, Idaho, Utah, and Arizona. He shares Wyoming, Colorado, and New Mexico with Giancanelli.
With 20 years in energy distribution, Hoover has worked as a journeyman lineman, lead and foreman.
“I used Hastings ’ products for my whole line career,” Hoover said, “So I know they make good products and stand by them.”
Finding ways to make the trade easier and safer is Hoover’s favorite part of being a Demonstrator.
Quaife, a former Marine based in Florida, joins Hastings with 20 years of journeyman lineman experience in transmission hot sticking and live line barehand and distribution, as well as 2 ½ years as a tool demonstrator elsewhere. He serves the East Coast, including states East of the Mississippi River, along with Hoover.
“As a Demonstrator, I get to travel around, work with customers and put our tools in people's hands so they can see them in action,” Quaife said. “I enjoy talking with customers, hearing about the work they do, and helping them find solutions that make their jobs easier.
“The best part of the job is meeting people from all over and being able to represent a company and products I believe in,” he added.
Roberts, also new to Hastings , is based in Florida and covers the East Coast, including states East of the Mississippi River, along with Quaife. He has 35 years of experience in energy distribution and as a first responder for transmission, including serving as a journeyman lineman, line trainer, lead line trainer, supervisor and manager.
He enjoys traveling the East Coast and beyond to share Hastings ’ products and suggest techniques for their use, care and maintenance. Solving problems experienced in the field is the most rewarding part of his role as a Hastings Demonstrator.
In addition to the regions and states specified for each Demonstrator, Alaska and Hawaii are covered by availability within the team.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic flags revenue surge to investors ahead of stock market debut
articles.title_zh: Anthropic flags revenue surge to investors ahead of stock market debut
articles.content_orig:
Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw its revenue surge by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.
The figures were revealed by the Claude-developer as it briefed prospective investors on Wednesday at its headquarters in San Francisco as it lays the groundwork for a stock market listing, which is expected to take place before the end of the year.
It comes as some tech stocks, including firms that make the chips and other hardware that power data centres, have fallen in recent days over concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure.
An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.
Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.
The company also reportedly said that it made a profit for the second quarter in a row.
Its revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, offer an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.
Stocks in some US technology companies fell on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.
Share in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.
In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank fell by more than 9% on Thursday morning. South Korean semiconductor giants were also down, with Samsung falling by 9.4% and SK Hynix dropping 10.8%.
Tech-heavy indexes in the region were also down. Trading on South Korea's Kospi and Kosdaq was temporarily halted after falling by more than 8%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 fell by over 5%.
The falls come after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending.
Tan said at an conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino".
There also been concerns over the safety of AI models.
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns about the technology's safety.
The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn.
Anthropic has also been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodei calling on the pace of development to slow down .
The company has continued expanding globally, opening an office in Singapore on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Global tech sell-off deepens as Asian markets tumble
articles.title_zh: Global tech sell-off deepens as Asian markets tumble
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A global sell-off in memory-chip stocks deepened overnight as South Korea's benchmark KOSPI ( ^KS11 ) tanked 7%.
Micron ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) were poised to open lower on Wednesday as SK Hynix ( 000660.KS ) and Samsung Electronics ( 005930.KS ) fell 10% and 8%, respectively, after tanking earlier this week over concerns about intensifying competition from China. The two memory giants account for more than half of the South Korean stock market's total capitalization.
The sell-off in South Korea followed a decline in the chip sector on Wall Street on Wednesday as worries about further rate hikes collided with fears of AI-driven debt financing.
Chip giant Nvidia ( NVDA ), Broadcom ( AVGO ), AMD ( AMD ), and Intel ( INTC ) all led the chip stocks lower during the session.
On Wednesday, worries about borrowing costs also hit the AI trade.
CoreWeave ( CRWV ) stock fell more than 15% after a chart of the neocloud providers' bond yields circulated on social media.
The stock's sharp sell-off highlighted concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet and whether it can scale fast enough to manage its growing interest expense.
Any slowdown in AI spending could spell trouble for chip makers, which have been the main beneficiaries of infrastructure spending as hyperscalers race to build out data centers.
On Thursday, investors will get another glimpse of the health of the AI buildout when TSMC ( TSM ) reports quarterly results. Investors expect quarterly profits to rise 60%.
Investors will pay close attention to the foundry's capacity, given ASML's ( ASML ) results on Wednesday. The maker of advanced chip-making machines warned it may not be able to fully meet demand in 2027 and 2008.
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Didn’t Pass Bar Exam
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Didn’t Pass Bar Exam
articles.content_orig:
A version of this story appeared in CNN’s What Matters newsletter. To get it in your inbox, sign up for free here .
The press secretary is supposed to spin the news, not be the news.
On that most essential qualification, the new lead White House spokeswoman, Katie Zacharia, is struggling.
She has presented herself as a lawyer but does not meet the requirements in her home state to use that title. And at least one watchdog group has asked the State Bar of California to investigate.
The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday , citing a person with direct knowledge of the matter, that Zacharia failed in an attempt to pass the California bar exam after graduating from law school.
Zacharia has a law degree from the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law. She also claims to have worked with appropriate credentials in China, but it’s not at all clear what credential she’s talking about.
While House spokesman Steven Cheung defended Zacharia in a statement.
“Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team,” he said. “She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary.”
These developments are made even more awkward after Republicans mercilessly attacked the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor, though he went to medical school and made his career in public health.
Squabbles over who can call themselves a lawyer or a doctor probably seem beside the point to a large portion of the country.
This issue here is not that a law degree is required to be White House press secretary — it isn’t.
The issue is that Zacharia has presented herself repeatedly on TV, including on CNN, as a lawyer, something the independent journalist Judd Legum first documented . Trump used the term “attorney” to describe her when he announced she would be his press secretary.
A review by CNN’s K-File found at least six instances when she referred to herself as either a lawyer or a corporate lawyer in her own words and multiple other instances in which she posted or reposted to social media using the term attorney or “legal strategist.”
Washington, DC, is filled to the brim with people who have law degrees but do not practice law. And it does not appear that Zacharia inappropriately tried to represent anyone in a court.
But all of this does suggest the vetting operation at the White House is, to be charitable, not very thorough.
When reporters asked Trump at the White House Tuesday where Zacharia passed the bar, she chimed in from behind him that she was when she moved to China. Even Trump did a double take.
She later clarified to The New York Times that she had misheard the question.
“I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” she said. “That’s all I could hear over the sound of Marine One,” she added, “and wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question.”
Zacharia later said in a statement she had “practiced international transactional law, with all the appropriate credentials.”
On her Linkedin page Zacharia lists herself as having worked as an “associate” in the international practice group at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing for nearly two years starting in 2011.
The Journal reported that she was one of four associates working as an “international legal consultant.”
Only citizens can become licensed to practice law in China, according to the Ministry of Justice , so it’s not clear what kind of credential she might have obtained.
“Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law,” according to a White House official.
In addition to saying on TV that she is a lawyer, Zacharia cites some other legal-sounding work on her LinkedIn page; for example, she lists herself as “general counsel” for the activist group Fix California. In the nonprofit group’s tax filing for 2024, Zacharia’s name appears as having been a fundraiser.
CNN’s White House team has found no evidence that Zacharia has passed the bar exam in the states where she has lived and worked since graduating from Pepperdine.
Here’s what California’s bar association told them:
California law lays out what’s required to be a lawyer.
There are requirements for college and law school, or their equivalents; for “good moral character”; passing an ethics exam; and passing the bar exam in California.
Zacharia, as a result, should not be considered a lawyer in California, the state where she has lived and worked.
A separate section of California law makes it a misdemeanor to pretend to be a lawyer.
Does presenting oneself as a lawyer on TV violate that piece of code?
The group Campaign for Accountability, which describes itself as a nonpartisan government watchdog, on Wednesday announced it had asked the State Bar of California to investigate.
None of that really matters to anyone who is more concerned with how the White House is handling the war Trump launched on Iran or the related inflation that continues to hit Americans in the wallet. Questions about whether Zacharia can call herself a lawyer, or not, mostly distract from those other, larger issues.
Ultimately, Trump is the person who speaks for his administration in the long, often rambling appearances he frequently makes in the Oval Office.
But those appearances may become less enjoyable for him in the future, especially if Democrats take control of one or both chambers of Congress and, as expected, launch a series of investigations into his administration, the money his family has made during his presidency, and much more.
He will, at that point, need a press secretary he can trust.
Questions about Zacharia’s CV are also an awkward development since Republicans in Michigan have attacked the Democrat running for Senate there, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor despite having gone to medical school.
At a debate this month, the Republican in the Senate race, former Rep. Mike Rogers, went so far as to say El-Sayed was a “con man.”
As CNN has reported , El-Sayed earned a Doctor of Medicine from Columbia University, but he does not practice clinical medicine.
El-Sayed has held public health positions in the Detroit area. His top policy issue is extending health insurance to all Americans.
Democratic boosters of El-Sayed have continued to call him a doctor.
“Abdul’s a doctor, and he’s taken on special interests to fight for good jobs, better healthcare, and lower costs,” former President Barack Obama said in an ad he cut for the Michigander.
CNN’s Kit Maher and Andrew Kaczynski contributed reporting.
This headline and story have been updated with additional reporting.

articles.title_orig: World War II event to be held in Hillsboro
articles.title_zh: World War II event to be held in Hillsboro
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. 2nd Rangers Infantry Battalion of St. Louis visited Hillsboro last year.
Jefferson County residents can step back in time this weekend at the 2026 World War II Weekend Living History event at the Jefferson County Fairgrounds, 10349 Business 21, in Hillsboro.
The nonprofit U.S. 2nd Rangers Infantry Battalion of St. Louis holds the event, which will include World War II reenactors staging military camps and battles from the European theatre. There is no admission fee.
This is the third year the event will be held in Jefferson County. It was established in the 1970s and previously was held at Jefferson Barracks Park in St. Louis County.
Festivities kick off on Friday with invasion history presented exclusively to local school groups at the fairgrounds. The event will be held from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday and 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Sunday.
Battle reenactments are set for 10:30 a.m. and 3 p.m. Saturday and 1 p.m. Sunday. Food vendors will be available on Saturday and Sunday.
Dan Dexter, president of the 2nd Rangers Infantry Battalion, said the weekend draws reenactors from across the region.
“We’ll have guys from Kansas, Missouri and Illinois. I think some guys are coming up from Kentucky,” he said.
A WWII Canteen Dance is set for 7-10 p.m. Saturday in the fairgrounds building. Dance tickets cost $20 at the door and $16 in advance through the U.S. 2nd Ranger Infantry Battalion of St. Louis Inc. Facebook page .
For more information, visit jeffersoncountyfair.net or the group’s Facebook page.

articles.title_orig: Billboard Magazine Names William Paterson University One of Its 2026 “Top Music Business Schools” in the World
articles.title_zh: Billboard Magazine Names William Paterson University One of Its 2026 “Top Music Business Schools” in the World
articles.content_orig:
Billboard magazine has once again placed William Paterson University on its list of “top music business schools” around the world—recognizing the University’s undergraduate program in music and entertainment industries.
William Paterson is one of only three New Jersey institutions on the list. This is the ninth time William Paterson has landed on the list, which includes schools throughout the United States, as well as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Spain.
In Billboard’s 2026 spotlight on colleges and universities educating the next generation of music business leaders, William Paterson’s program in music and entertainment industries was noted for its balance between the classroom and real-world experiences. Courses evolve with industry trends. The popular course Personal Management in the Music and Entertainment Industry explores topics from the evolution of social media and AI to the lessening impact of major labels and the rise of artist independence. Students also participate in a variety of industry events, from Grammy U and New York Music Week to the jump. Global VOLUMES summit and more.
Billboard chooses its top music business schools based on industry recommendations, alumni information provided by honorees from its multiple power lists, information requested from each school, and more than a decade of reporting on educational options. All programs on the list are campus-based and bestow bachelor’s or associate degrees.
“Recognition from Billboard proves that the William Paterson University ‘s music and entertainment industries program is more than relevant in a new world where AI fears and go-it-alone artists are the foundation for the music business,” says David Kirk Philp, assistant professor of music and coordinator of the program. “We teach, we listen, we provide guidance. Ultimately, it is our program’s responsibility to help students and the next generation of artists and executives navigate past the fear and embrace what we see as opportunity. We’re forward looking while keeping an eye on what really matters: providing tools for success both on and off stage. That is our mission and the Billboard recognition shows we’re on the right track.”
William Paterson offers a bachelor of music degree with an emphasis in music and entertainment industries, open to students studying classical or jazz performance, as well as a minor in music and entertainment industries open to students from any major. Courses include Entrepreneurship in the Music and Entertainment Industry, in which students write a business plan for a new company; other offerings focus on the importance of social media and marketing. Internships are the backbone of the program. Students are encouraged to apply for internships beginning the summer after freshman year, and to take advantage of the University’s commuting distance to New York City.
In addition, the highly popular Music Biz 101 & More radio show and podcast, produced by Philp and Dr. Stephen Marcone, William Paterson professor emeritus of music, is the only free advice talk show in America that focuses on the business side of the music and entertainment worlds, with more than 300 episodes available to stream online.
Graduates of the program are represented in all areas of the music and entertainment industry, from independent recording artists to record labels, music publishing, concert promotion and venues, and with top artists such as Khalid and Tyler, the Creator.

articles.title_orig: Iran-backed Houthis strike Saudi oil company Aramco’s headquarters, officials say
articles.title_zh: Iran-backed Houthis strike Saudi oil company Aramco’s headquarters, officials say
articles.content_orig:
A building owned by the energy giant Aramco was set ablaze late Tuesday in a strike on the Saudi city housing its headquarters, the kingdom’s energy ministry said, as war spiked between the Houthi militia in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis had threatened earlier in the day to attack the Aramco headquarters in the eastern city of Dhahran, but did not immediately take responsibility for the strike. It came after the Iranian-backed militia reported that two major oil facilities in Yemen had been attacked by Saudi forces on Tuesday.
The Saudi energy ministry said in a statement that the strike in Dhahran had hit an Aramco administrative building and caused “a limited fire” and no injuries.
By late Tuesday, residents of both countries were on edge as explosions were repeatedly heard in their capital cities. A Saudi-led coalition said it was targeting Yemeni facilities that support the Houthi war effort, while the Houthis vowed to retaliate against comparable sites in Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi authorities issued warnings of an aerial threat in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. And Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said four cruise missiles fired toward Riyadh and southern Saudi Arabia had been intercepted, along with two drones.
Mr. al-Maliki also reported that a ballistic missile launched toward the city of Damman in the eastern part of the kingdom by the Houthis had been intercepted, and that shrapnel fell in a residential area of neighboring Dhahran.

articles.content_orig:
The iPhone Duo unsurprisingly offers performance similar to the iPhone 18 Pro , according to an early iPhone Duo benchmark shared on Geekbench 7. Both devices are equipped with Apple's 2nm A20 Pro chip with a 6-core CPU and a 7-core GPU.
The benchmarked ‌iPhone Duo‌ (iPhone19,4) is running iOS 27.1, as expected, and it had a single-core score of 3986 and a multi-core score of 11067. That's in line with multiple benchmarks collected from ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ and ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max models.
Scores vary from test to test, so while the result does fall short of the top ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ benchmark scores, we're only viewing a single score. The ‌iPhone Duo‌ has the same 6-core CPU with a 4.93GHz base frequency that's identified in ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ benchmarks, and it lists 11.30GB memory, which means 12GB of RAM.
While the ‌iPhone Duo‌ and ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ models use the same A20 Pro chip, there could be differences in real-world performance based on thermal management, the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s two screens vs. a single screen, and other factors.
Apple says the A20 Pro offers up to 20 percent faster CPU performance than the A19 Pro and up to 40 percent faster GPU performance. GPU speeds were not tested.
Pre-orders for the ‌iPhone Duo‌ will start on October 16, and a launch will follow on October 23.

articles.title_orig: A long-term perspective on humanity’s battle against malaria
articles.title_zh: A long-term perspective on humanity’s battle against malaria
articles.content_orig:
According to the latest data from the World Health Organization, the global death rate from malaria has almost halved since the year 2000.
The chart above puts this recent progress into a larger historical perspective. It combines the latest estimates from the WHO and the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation with those for the 20th century published by the late malaria researcher Richard Carter. Since 1900, the global death rate has declined by 96%. If it were still as high as it was then, around 16 million people would die from malaria every year instead of 610,000.
Behind this long-run decline is a shift in the distribution of the burden of malaria. In the first half of the 20th century, most malaria victims died in the Asian tropics. It was the substantial progress there — as well as in the Mediterranean and in the Americas — that made this vast improvement in human health possible.
Today, more than 9 out of 10 malaria deaths occur in Africa. This means that the recent progress shown in the chart is, above all, Africa’s progress.
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
China is often the poster child for rapid reductions in poverty, and for good reason. In the early 1980s, over 90% of its population lived in extreme poverty, but by the early 2020s, that number had dropped to nearly zero.
Some might assume that China is the only reason why global extreme poverty has declined. But that’s wrong : many countries have seen dramatic reductions in poverty, too. Indonesia is one clear example; it’s shown alongside China on the chart.
In 1984, 86% of Indonesians lived on less than $3 per day. By 2025, this had fallen to less than 4%. While it didn’t quite match China’s decline, it has still been impressive. The number of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from 140 million to about 10 million.
Note that the international poverty line is extremely low, defined as people living on less than $3 per day. But Indonesia has also made progress when measuring higher poverty lines .
Many of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from:
Almost nine in ten people picked B or C, thinking it was more than one-third.
The correct answer was A: around 0.5% of plastic waste ends up in the ocean.
The chart shows how the OECD gets to this number. Globally, we produce around 350 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. Most of this is managed responsibly, either in secure landfills, through recycling, or incineration. But around one-quarter of it is mismanaged or littered.
From there, a decreasing fraction of plastic waste leaks to the environment, then into rivers and coastlines, and finally into the ocean. Around 1.7 million tonnes end up there: around 0.5% of what was generated in the first place.
People tend to think that most of our plastic ends up there, but only a tiny percentage does. This should make plastic pollution an easier problem to solve: we already know how to manage most of it well. The challenge is to ensure that all plastic is handled this way.
The new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart.
Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it.
I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct.
But it tells us none of that.
It examines changes across nearly 36,000 animal populations and reports the average change. This gets even more complicated because it’s based on a geometric mean, and populations get weighted differently in the final index.
When we look a bit deeper, we see that not all populations are doing poorly. As shown in the chart, around half have declined, while the other half have either increased in abundance or remained stable.
As I explained in a previous article , being able to identify which of these populations is doing particularly badly is crucial if we’re to focus our conservation efforts on where they’re needed most.
In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.
The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.
In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.
Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.
And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.
The median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises.
That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates.
The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42.
But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. It rose by a third, from 23 to 31 years, in a bit less than a generation.
Europe’s population is older, but the median age has been rising more quickly in Latin America this century. That’s largely due to fertility falling later and faster in the latter.

articles.title_orig: Could the Taliban’s new road to China drive negotiating power?
articles.title_zh: Could the Taliban’s new road to China drive negotiating power?
articles.content_orig:
Badakhshan Province, 4 October 2026, covering the Wakhan Corridor and Pamir region in Afghanistan (Javid Ashna via Getty Images)
In treacherous terrain, the Taliban has carved a path to potentially strengthen its position with China and against Pakistan.
Subscribe to The Informer for monthly expert analysis, and to Events for advance notice of visiting world leaders and distinguished guests.
You may unsubscribe from Lowy Institute newsletters at any time. For information on our privacy practices and how to unsubscribe, see our Privacy Policy .
Could the Taliban’s new road to China drive negotiating power?
The Taliban regime in Afghanistan has spent 365 million Afghanis – about US$5.5 million – building a road through one of the most remote corners of the country towards the Chinese border. It may turn out to be little more than a rough mountain road. But it could also give Afghanistan something it lacks: leverage.
At the northeastern edge of Afghanistan in the Wakhan Corridor, (Opens in new window) this new road is quietly changing the strategic geography. The Taliban's Ministry of Rural Rehabilitation and Development inaugurated (Opens in new window) the 121-kilometre gravel road on 4 October 2026, running from Broghil in Wakhan district to China’s border. The route includes four bridges, 66 culverts and more than 3,000 metres of retaining walls.
The road does not yet mean that Afghan trucks can simply drive into China, and there is no commercial border crossing. But it brings Afghanistan physically closer to a country that has become increasingly important to the Taliban's regional diplomacy. That possibility matters.
For years, Afghanistan has depended heavily on Pakistan for access to international markets. That dependence has become uncomfortable as relations between Kabul and Islamabad have deteriorated. The two countries shut major border crossings after deadly fighting in October 2025, disrupting bilateral trade and leaving hundreds of trucks stranded. The closure exposed how vulnerable Afghanistan remains to decisions made by its neighbour.
The consequences have gone beyond trade and impacts citizens. Before the closure, more than 70% (Opens in new window) of medicines used in Afghanistan were imported from Pakistan, according to the European Union Agency for Asylum. So, the attraction of another route is obvious.
The Wakhan Corridor is a narrow strip of Afghan territory extending eastwards between Tajikistan and Pakistan before reaching China's Xinjiang region. Its strategic importance is hardly new (Opens in new window) . During the 19th century’s Great Game era, it served as a buffer between the British Empire in India and the Russian Empire to the north.
The mountains that once made Wakhan useful as a buffer also made it extraordinarily difficult to reach. High passes, severe winters and poor infrastructure have kept the corridor isolated. The new road does not change that geography, but it does begin to work around it, and Beijing has been paying attention.
In February, Afghanistan's ambassador to China, Mawlawi Asadullah Bilal Karimi, met Liu Jinsong, head of the Department of Asian Affairs at China's foreign ministry. According to Chinese and Afghan accounts, the discussions included China-Afghanistan relations. Afghan reporting also said activation of the Wakhan Corridor was discussed.
In March, Afghanistan’s Acting Minister of Commerce Nooruddin Azizi also met China's Special Representative in Kabul, Yu Xiaoyong (Opens in new window) in Kabul to discuss connectivity and transit.
While this demonstrates diplomacy around the idea, there is a distinction between a road reaching China, and China agreeing to open a full commercial crossing. Beijing has made no public commitment to do so, and that is likely to remain the challenge.
A functioning trade route would require customs facilities, security arrangements and infrastructure, as well as a road capable of handling sustained commercial traffic. A high-altitude gravel road through the Pamirs is a different proposition from a modern trade corridor.
China's calculations are likely to be cautious for another reason: security. (Opens in new window) Beijing has maintained pragmatic relations with the Taliban while stressing its concerns about militant groups operating from Afghan territory, particularly those that could threaten China's Xinjiang region. China has also supported security cooperation along the Wakhan frontier. In 2025, China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi (Opens in new window) said Beijing supported the resumption of bilateral patrols in the corridor and called for stronger Afghan action against the East Turkestan Islamic Movement and other militant groups.
For Beijing, therefore, the road is not simply about moving goods. It is also about what happens in the mountains beside Xinjiang. This is where the road becomes more interesting than its modest size suggests.
The new road does not change that geography, but it does begin to work around it, and Beijing has been paying attention.
Afghanistan has long been described as a potential bridge between Central Asia, China, South Asia and the Middle East. Its geography offers that possibility, but decades of war, political instability and inadequate infrastructure have prevented it from becoming reality. The Taliban now appears determined to test that proposition. (Opens in new window)
The most ambitious possibility would be a wider network linking China through Afghanistan to Iran and the Arabian Sea. Afghanistan already has access to Iran's Chabahar port, which offers an alternative to Pakistan's seaports. But that route has also been subject to geopolitical uncertainty, making the search for multiple routes more significant. But it would be a mistake to portray the Wakhan road as a ready-made alternative to Pakistan's ports, as the road is only the first piece of a larger puzzle.
Beijing may see value in greater economic access to Afghanistan. It may also see strategic value in having another potential connection to Central Asia and the wider region. But China has shown little appetite for taking unnecessary risks in Afghanistan. The road therefore matters less because it guarantees trade than because it creates possibility.
For Kabul, the symbolism is powerful. The Taliban can point to a domestically funded infrastructure project reaching towards China at a time when Afghanistan remains internationally isolated. More practically, it gives Kabul a card to play in its difficult relationship with Pakistan.
Shadi Khan Saif is a Melbourne-based journalist and a former Afghanistan/Pakistan correspondent for Reuters and Deutsche Welle.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq ends sharply lower as hot inflation data stirs rate-hike worries
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq ends sharply lower as hot inflation data stirs rate-hike worries
articles.content_orig:
U.S. consumers are in the midst of one of the longest stretches of elevated inflation of the past century. Some are beginning to act like it's a new normal, raising alarm bells for members of the Federal Reserve .
Wednesday's consumer price index release showed a 3.7% increase year over year in September. CPI has now registered around 65 months — that's more than five years — of consecutive annual readings above 2%, a widely accepted target for inflation in the U.S.
This yearslong spell of high inflation has cast a dark cloud over everyday Americans' view of the economy, and could shape everything from how they budget to how they vote in next month's midterm elections. At the Fed, leaders are left questioning whether consumers' inflationary expectations are becoming too entrenched to rein in.
"They're starting to accept high inflation as just a fact of life," Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wrote in a social media post last week. "That's concerning."
The current streak of stubborn inflation ranks among the most persistent in modern U.S. history.
The uninterrupted string of above-2% monthly CPI readings is the longest of the 21st century, according to a CNBC analysis of data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The U.S. has seen longer periods on only two other occasions going back to the late 1940s.
Since inflation started running above 2% in early 2021, the average CPI reading has sat around 4.5%. The last time a streak had a mean reading that high was during a period ending in the 1980s .
Consumers are expecting inflation to accelerate. The one-year inflation outlook in September rose three-tenths of a percentage point to 3.9%, its highest reading in more than three years, according to the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations released last week.
One of the main worries of central bankers is that businesses and consumers may start permanently adjusting their behaviors to account for high prices. That can have ripple effects through the economy.
Businesses anticipating rising costs can preemptively hike prices for consumers. Workers expecting sticky inflation will ask for steeper pay raises to get ahead of any sticker shock.
All of this can make inflation a self-fulfilling prophecy, rendering the monetary policy tools at the Fed's disposal less effective in slowing price growth.
"Inflation expectations have to be anchored for monetary policy to affect the economy in an effective and predictable manner," said Gary Richardson, an economist and former historian at the Fed. "That's got to be number-one goal of any central bank."
At this juncture, Fed officials are closely watching to see if and how consumers respond to inflationary pressures.
During an event last month, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said he heard from a labor union leader that inflation was "worse" than a recession for their members. Kashkari said that conversation influenced how he views the trade-off within the Fed's so-called dual mandate, which calls for stability in prices and maximum employment.
At a gathering of economists in Ohio this week, Hammack told the audience that she did not take the fact that long-run inflation expectations have stayed anchored "for granted." With each month that inflation comes in high, she warned that the risk grows of an "inflationary mindset" getting entrenched.
Economists widely view interest rate hikes as the Fed's main mechanism for slowing demand and, in turn, putting downward pressure on the annual pace of price growth. After hiking interest rates in September , Fed funds futures traders anticipate the central bank will raise borrowing costs further in December and in 2027.
In the long run, Diane Swonk, chief economist at consultancy KPMG, said interest rate hikes can benefit consumers by getting inflation under control. But in the near term, Swonk said consumers can feel more pressure due to higher borrowing costs.
"Inflation is like a cancer, and if you let it metastasize and go further, it's even worse," Swonk said. "Even when the cure hurts, it's better than letting it metastasize."
In Hammack's district, the Cleveland Fed chief said via social media that she's found evidence that residents are "choosing" rather than "trading down." For instance, she said they need to pick whether to pay for groceries or essential bills.
Consumers have lamented the cumulative price increases they now see in everyday life after the years-long run of high inflation. Adding to their woes is the fact that year-over-year inflation has run at a faster clip than wage growth in recent months, meaning the average consumer has lost purchasing power.
The University of Michigan's closely followed consumer sentiment survey earlier this year fell to the lowest levels ever seen . The highest share of respondents citing high prices as a reason for having worse personal finances surpassed 50% for the first time on record in 2026.
High prices are "dominating consumer thinking," said Joanne Hsu, the director of Michigan's survey. "They still consider it an unacceptable fact of life."
Compared with Democrats, consumer sentiment has tumbled more sharply among Republicans and independents this year. The question now is if voters angered about the rising cost of living will shift control in Washington away from Republicans and President Donald Trump in the midterm election.
Despite those glum outlooks, economists say that everyday Americans shouldn't bank on prices coming down from current levels. Deflation — which is when annual price growth falls below 0% — could put the national economy on a downward spiral.
Instead, their hope should be that inflation's 12-month growth rate can cool to levels below the pace of pay increases. If that happens for a long enough period, the higher wages and increased purchasing power would leave shoppers better equipped for today's prices.
Olena Nicks, an analyst and local lawmaker in Long Island, New York, is one of those consumers tightening the purse strings in the face of lofty prices. Nicks said she's specifically noticed steep price increases over recent years in the grocery store produce aisle and when looking at airline flights for vacations.
In response, the 34-year-old said she's cut back on purchasing meals at restaurants or from fast-food chains. Her friend group has forgone leisure activities like bowling, opting instead for less-costly nights spent in someone's home.
"Frustrated is an understatement," Nicks said. "It feels like you're stuck."

articles.title_orig: Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago
articles.title_zh: Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago
articles.content_orig:
Alleged assault follows report of gang-rape at frat house at Cornell, which ignited national uproar and criticism online
A 21-year-old woman reported being sexually assaulted last weekend at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago , as Greek life nationwide faces renewed scrutiny for recurrent misconduct.
The incident allegedly took place on Sunday at about 1.50am at the off-campus Alpha Epsilon Pi residence, according to a university daily crime log.
In a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times, the woman said she was “not fully conscious” when she was found partially undressed inside a bathroom with a man, who was also semi-nude.
She told police, according to the report, that a group had blocked her friends, at first, from entering the bathroom.
A person of interest has been identified, according to university officials.
The individual is not a student and has been banned from campus, they announced on Wednesday.
No one is in custody, Chicago police said on Wednesday afternoon, adding that an investigation remains ongoing.
Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity, said on Wednesday there was no evidence its members had participated in the assault or were aware of it.
“When AEPi members (there were several “sober monitors” during the party, including the chapter’s safety officer) became aware of the victim’s report, they offered assistance by providing food and water and even loaned a shirt to the victim as she reported being cold while she waited outside for emergency response,” Pierce said.
“We are pleased that the alleged assailant has been identified and hope that the victim can find some solace in knowing that justice is being done.”
The alleged assault follows a harrowing report of a gang-rape at a Cornell University fraternity house in 2024. Recent news of the purported attack ignited national uproar and criticism of the Ivy League school’s perceived leniency toward the alleged offenders.
New York state prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the report.
Under mounting backlash, Cornell has also suspended all fraternity parties for the remainder of the academic year, as it assesses the safety of its Greek societies.
Last week, the University of Arizona took a similar move, halting all fraternity activity in the wake of several hazing and physical assault allegations, including accusations of a Greek organization coercing recruits into binge drinking and swallowing live goldfish.

articles.title_orig: SC US Senate campaign escalates on China, law enforcement
articles.title_zh: SC US Senate campaign escalates on China, law enforcement
articles.content_orig:
On Wednesday, the war of words ramped up across the Palmetto State between U.S. Senate candidates, Republican Sen. Darline Graham and her Democratic challenger, Dr. Annie Andrews.
The candidates held dueling events in the Lowcountry and Upstate, as they look to get any edge with undecided voters in a race recent polls show is a close contest.
The increasingly heated campaign rhetoric and back-and-forth tied to China, foreign policy, and law enforcement comes less than a week before the start of early voting and less than three weeks until Election Day.
“National security isn’t an elective in this job," Andrews said during an event Wednesday morning in Charleston. There, she cited a recent Washington Post report that claimed Graham's husband is an executive at a company connected to Chinese weapons manufacturing.
Andrews said that the senator's family should cut any business ties to China and that Graham should recuse herself from any votes involving trade with China or Chinese military policy.
“I think it’s just important that we always put America first, American interests first, American security interests, privacy interests, data security interests, first and foremost," Andrews said. "To me, it’s a non-story; I mean, she’s desperate obviously," Graham said, who responded to Andrews' claims at an event Wednesday afternoon in Spartanburg — and pushed back on the claims in the Washington Post article.
"Bringing my husband into this is absolutely wrong; he’s an employee at a company," Graham said. "He doesn’t own it, he doesn’t have any shares in the company, he’s never been to China, he doesn’t make decisions like that, so I think it’s completely unfair to my husband.” On Wednesday afternoon in Greenville, several sheriffs of Upstate counties also officially endorsed Graham, citing her commitment to law enforcement funding.
“We understand her support for law enforcement," Greenville County Sheriff Hobart Lewis said.
In response, an Andrews campaign spokesperson said Graham failed to sign on to legislation that would help police officers buy homes and strengthen collective bargaining protections.

articles.title_orig: Did Katie Zacharia pass the bar exam? What we know about her legal credentials
articles.title_zh: Did Katie Zacharia pass the bar exam? What we know about her legal credentials
articles.content_orig:
In October, social media posts questioned new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia's claim that she passed the bar examination in China.
The posts emerged after several reports asked whether Zacharia had the credentials to practice law anywhere in the U.S., though she has repeatedly identified herself as a lawyer in the past, including in an archived version of her X profile and during a television interview .
When asked Oct. 13 where she passed the bar (the examination that allows people to practice law), Zacharia responded , "When I moved to China." She did not say she passed the bar in any U.S. state.
People on Facebook and Reddit expressed doubts, while Rep. Ted Lieu, a Democrat from California, wrote on X, " Are Katie Zacharia and trump lying when they say she is an attorney? " ( archived ):
Meanwhile, Snopes readers emailed and searched the website, asking us to examine whether Zacharia could have possibly passed the bar in China.
An extensive search turned up no evidence Zacharia was a member of any state bar in the U.S., nor in Washington, D.C. In addition, current Chinese law made it unlikely that she was ever in a position to pass China's examination to practice law, as she is not a Chinese national. There was no evidence that she could do when she lived there between 2011 and 2013, though China only formalized rules about foreign lawyers in 2017.
For this reason, we have left the claim unrated.
"I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Katie Zacharia told Snopes in an emailed statement. Neither she nor the White House press office answered follow-up questions, nor did they share any documentation showing she could practice law as an attorney in good standing in any jurisdiction.
" Katie graduated with a JD [Juris Doctor, a law degree] from Caruso School of Law in 2011, and with a bachelor of arts in political science from Seaver College in 2007," a spokesperson for Pepperdine University wrote in an email to Snopes.
A sked whether Zacharia could have taken and passed China's law examination before 2017, John Ohnesorge , a law professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who researched Chinese regulations of lawyers, said in an email to Snopes, "There's no possibility that she passed the Chinese bar exam, ever."
"W hat she did in China was to work in an elite Chinese law firm on international business matters, and doing that kind of work does not really require being a member of a bar anywhere," he added.
We also searched lawyer directories across the U.S. and found no record of Katie Zacharia — also searching by her maiden name, Black — in any of them.
Zacharia's LinkedIn profile indicates she worked in China between 2011 and 2013, at Zhong Lun Law Firm .
In 2020, the Chinese Justice Observer — a consulting platform and analysis outlet about the Chinese legal system — said foreigners cannot practice law in China . In 2019, China established a pilot program to allow foreign lawyers to act as legal consultants in China, not lawyers, though one condition is that the person should have practiced as a lawyer in their home country for at least two years.
Even under this program, Zacharia could not have practiced as a legal consultant as she had not practiced law in the U.S. long enough after she graduated.
Zacharia's LinkedIn indicates she later worked as "general counsel" for Fix California , a conservative organization that aims at ensuring "election integrity." It is unclear how she could hold this position without having passed the state's bar examination. We reached out to Fix California asking for more details.
A sheet of advice for French lawyers seeking to work in China from 2017 confirms that only Chinese nationals can practice law in China. In other words, any foreign lawyer practicing in China can do so only with credentials from the countries where they obtained their degrees.
However, China's current rules were implemented in 2017 . Ohnesorge, who wrote a research paper in 2023 about the history of the regulation of lawyers in China, said this measure was most likely protectionistic.
"It's true that the 2017 regulation started requiring two years of practice in a home jurisdiction in order to qualify as a foreign legal consultant, but that's best understood as a protectionist measure used to keep Chinese firms from hiring too many foreign lawyers, not a requirement that actually makes any sense," Ohnesorge said via email. "People doing the work she did aren't really practicing the law of their home jurisdiction anyway, so why require that at all?"
For further reading, Snopes covered several rumors about Zacharia's predecessor, Karoline Leavitt , including the claim that she said the war in Iran would be over if President Donald Trump had "better intelligence."

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's Starlink restrictions raise suspicions of Musk, Trump retaliation
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's Starlink restrictions raise suspicions of Musk, Trump retaliation
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said Wednesday that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump was responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network.
Writing on X, Musk said that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Ukraine had accused SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on the Starshield internet service without warning, leading to disruptions to Ukrainian military operations amid fresh Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
On Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said SpaceX had implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion, without notifying the country's defense forces.
That had disrupted some missions, and the same restrictions also applied to Starshield, he said on Telegram . Starlink is used to operate Ukraine's interceptor drones, the "most effective solution" against Moscow's Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said.
Starshield is a military-grade satellite network, while Starlink is only meant for "civilian or defensive activities," Musk said.
Some restrictions appear to have been partially lifted, with former Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov thanking Musk early Thursday morning that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers an hour had been restored. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," Fedorov added.
The developments come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over an "energy ceasefire," between Ukraine and Russia announced by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukraine has, however, welcomed a deal subject to Moscow honoring its commitment, while Russian authorities said talks were ongoing, without confirming whether they had reached an agreement. On Monday, Zelenskyy accused the Russians of breaching the ceasefire.
Trump had also taken aim at Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities, saying that Kyiv's attacks were responsible for the increase in diesel prices, instead of the U.S.' war with Iran.
Washington has threatened to cut intelligence sharing with Kyiv, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Ukrainian officials said a day earlier that they have not received warnings of Russian attacks on the country for two straight days.
— CNBC's Elsa Olhen contributed to this report.
