articles.title_orig: Dozens of California dams need repair as El Niño winter draws closer
articles.title_zh: Dozens of California dams need repair as El Niño winter draws closer
articles.content_orig:
With an El Niño winter threatening heavy rain, the State Auditor warns that California’s aging dams “continue to pose a risk to public safety,” especially in the Bay Area, San Diego, and Los Angeles areas.
Lawmakers gave the state the power to penalize dam owners that violate safety requirements in 2017, after the Oroville spillway failure forced the evacuation of nearly 200,000 people. Water managers have yet to use that power, the audit found.
Even if state water managers had wielded their enforcement powers, dam owners likely couldn’t have afforded the fixes.
An audit released Monday found 57 dams in poor or unsatisfactory condition as of May, up from previous counts. That number is likely to keep rising, as state water officials reevaluate aging dams.
The 40 riskiest dams — rated high or extremely high hazard — are located throughout the state, but cluster near densely populated coastal cities.
Should these dams fail, the auditor reported, “they could collectively endanger as many as 1.5 million people and cause more than $265 billion in economic damage.”
Almost a decade ago, lawmakers strengthened the California Department of Water Resources’ authority to impose penalties such as reservoir restrictions, property liens, and fines when dam owners violate state safety laws and other requirements.
State engineers have referred owners of 44 dams for enforcement as of April. But, the auditor wrote, the water resources department “has never taken punitive enforcement actions against dam owners that fail to remedy their violations.”
The problem is that dams are getting older. Many were built when safety standards were softer. State laws never required dam owners to set aside funds to keep them safe, so when concrete crumbles, sediment accumulates and spillways threaten to erode under floodwaters, most dam owners lack the money for repairs.
The state’s water resources department oversees the safety of more than 1,220 dams, most of them in satisfactory condition. Responsibility for maintaining the dams falls to the local governments, utilities, water agencies, and the private landowners and companies that own them. Some of the dams rated in poor condition are owned by state agencies.
Disasters are extremely rare. But when they do occur, like in Oroville, or the 1928 collapse of nearly-new St. Francis dam northwest of Los Angeles — they can be catastrophic.
The auditor applauded the water resources department’s inspection program but blasted its failure to enforce against dam owners who fail to meet state planning, safety or other requirements, “thereby allowing serious deficiencies to persist.”
One of the cases involved a dam with a 47-foot-wide hole in its spillway that has gone unrepaired for more than 30 years, which the audit said could cause flooding affecting nearly 300 people and more than $88 million in damage.
The audit doesn’t name the dam. State water managers said more specifics could pose security concerns, though the department makes each dam’s hazard potential and condition public in an annual report.
State water managers finalized the enforcement regulations in 2022. But they told the auditor they haven’t been able to adequately staff an enforcement branch and aren’t confident they could afford to defend their actions in a hearing.
Even with staff and money, the auditor concludes, if a dam owner remained noncompliant, the state “cannot act before the dam poses emergency-level danger. This leaves a gap in state law that puts public safety at risk.”
Gov. Gavin Newsom touted dam repairs in his drought-era water supply strategy four years ago, as a way to shore up water supplies. Two years later, in 2024, Newsom and lawmakers slashed funding for a dam repair grant program.
Since then, a 2024 ballot proposition delivered a $464 million infusion for the program. A Federal Emergency Management Agency grant also awarded California $629,198 this September, according to Jason Ince, a spokesperson for the Department of Water Resources.
But the audit cited estimates that repairing the state’s less-than-satisfactory dams could cost around $28 billion, making the funding a drop in the bucket.
The report urged state lawmakers to set deadlines and require dam owners with high and extremely high hazard dams — meaning ones that could kill people if they fail — to submit maintenance and repair plans to state agencies.
It also called for lawmakers to expand state water managers’ enforcement authority, and for the agency to use the full force of its powers.
“To ensure that the safety of the public is addressed before a dam’s condition results in an emergency,” the audit said, “the Legislature should amend state law to allow Water Resources to order the condemnation and decommissioning of a dam when Water Resources’ other means of enforcement are unsuccessful.”
Laura Hollender, deputy director of flood management and safety with the Department of Water Resources, said that the department worked closely with the State Auditor but disagrees with some of the report’s findings and recommendations.
Still, she said in a statement, they are carefully reviewing the recommendations and preparing for whatever El Niño brings. “Protecting public safety is DWR’s highest priority, and we recognize the critical role that dam safety and levee maintenance play in reducing flood risk for California communities.”
As the wet season approaches, the auditor also highlighted that dam safety planning statewide is incomplete.
The Governor’s Office of Emergency Service has not yet approved emergency plans for 245 dams describing what their owners would do to protect people and property should the dam fail. Officials told the auditor’s office that dam owners haven’t completed required revisions, and state law doesn’t require deadlines.
This story was originally published by CalMatters and distributed through a partnership with The Associated Press.

articles.title_orig: NC A&T alumnus matriculates ‘A Different World’ reboot
articles.title_zh: NC A&T alumnus matriculates ‘A Different World’ reboot
articles.content_orig:
North Carolina A&T State University alumnus Joshua Suiter is a Hillman College Falcon, too.
Suiter, a 2022 A&T graduate and a former Mister A&T, stars in the Netflix reboot of “A Different World.” The sitcom, which debuted at No. 1 on the streaming platform in the U.S., has been renewed for a second season. It builds on the cultural impact of the original NBC series (1987-93), which helped shape a cultural boom connected to Black college life.
Following a new generation of students at the fictional Hillman College, the sequel explores college life while examining the legacy of students who came before them. Suiter portrays Andre, a classmate of Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), daughter of original characters Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison).
“Seeing all the love for Andre really hit home,” Suiter said. “He’s one of my favorite characters thus far, and we created him from scratch, so to know that the hard work is being received and folks want more encourages me to keep going.”
Suiter discovered acting and musical theater at 7, and eventually matriculated at A&T, where he earned a degree in professional theater. Suiter was a standout in the performing arts on campus, where one of his more notable performances was in “Ain’t Misbehavin’” in 2019 where he first met Guy. In addition to acting, Suiter worked as a theater technician and developed skills in entertainment marketing and business.
“I came in as a creative, but what A&T did between Alpha Phi Alpha, the classes, talking business with professors and serving as Mister A&T sharpened me on the business side,” he said. “It sharpened my networking skills while showing me how to be authentic to who I am.”
Suiter, who appeared in the Hulu series “All’s Fair,” considers “A Different World” a full-circle moment as a Black college alumnus playing a role in the reboot.
“When you talk about an HBCU experience, I’m putting mine up there with the best of them,” he said. “I have so many experiences to pull from with the run of this show, with the character Andre. Hillman even has a heartbeat of its own, so it’s been fun exploring what that feels like as a student there, while still carrying that Aggie Pride in my heart.”

articles.title_orig: ICE officer appeared to intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston, Texas prosecutor says
articles.title_zh: ICE officer appeared to intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston, Texas prosecutor says
articles.content_orig:
Brittany Taylor , Senior Digital Content Producer
Xavier James , Photojournalist
HOUSTON – One of two men who were handcuffed inside an Immigration and Customs Enforcement SUV when an agent struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez has now been identified, and his attorney says he could be a key witness in the criminal investigation.
The new information came Wednesday during a news conference held by FIEL Houston, attorneys and family members of Parra-Hernandez, the 48-year-old man seriously injured during an ICE operation near Highway 6 and Clay Road on Oct. 10.
Attorney Kim Bruno said she represents both Parra-Hernandez and Luis Enriquez, one of the two men detained inside the SUV when the collision occurred.
“He was cuffed in the vehicle at the time of this incident, and so he is a key witness,” Bruno said.
Bruno said the Harris County District Attorney’s Office is working to obtain Enriquez’s statement.
FIEL Houston Executive Director Cesar Espinosa said both men who were inside the SUV are now being held at a detention facility in Montgomery County.
The developments come as District Attorney Sean Teare investigates whether the ICE agent intentionally struck Parra-Hernandez and whether critical evidence was lost when the agent drove the SUV away before investigators could examine it.
Until Wednesday, prosecutors had publicly discussed the presence of two detained individuals inside the SUV, but little was known about who they were.
Now, one of those men has been identified as Luis Enriquez.
Bruno said Enriquez has firsthand knowledge of what happened when the ICE vehicle struck Parra-Hernandez.
Espinosa said both detained men were inside the SUV during the events leading up to the collision and could provide information about what the agent did.
Their firsthand accounts have not yet been made public.
Enriquez’s sister, Nidia, also spoke at Wednesday’s news conference.
She said her brother was on his way to breakfast with his employees before work when ICE stopped them.
According to Nidia, her brother has lived in the United States for 34 years, owns a small business and employs people from the community.
She also said he has no outstanding arrest warrants or criminal history and has an approved immigration case while awaiting a green card.
KPRC 2 has not independently verified those immigration and criminal-history details.
Nidia said her family is frightened about what could happen to Enriquez while he remains detained, particularly now that he has been identified as a potential witness.
“My brother is afraid. My parents are afraid. We all as family are afraid, but we are speaking up and we are asking the community to step up,” she said.
She also urged others who witnessed the incident to contact investigators.
While investigators work to obtain witness statements, Parra-Hernandez remains hospitalized with serious injuries.
FIEL Houston says his right leg was fractured in multiple places and his left leg was also injured.
Bruno said Parra-Hernandez still needs another operation on his ankle and cannot put weight on his injured leg.
But attorneys say they are concerned ICE may attempt to transfer him to a detention facility before he completes his medical treatment.
Bruno said there were discussions Tuesday about moving him out of the hospital.
She also said the Harris County Sheriff’s Office contacted authorities to request that Parra-Hernandez remain hospitalized so he could continue recovering and undergo the additional surgery.
That account of the sheriff’s office intervention has not been independently confirmed.
“We do not understand the haste that ICE has to move Mr. Miguel Parra to a detention facility,” Espinosa said.
Espinosa and Bruno argued that a transfer could jeopardize Parra-Hernandez’s recovery.
Bruno also said ICE officers have made it difficult for attorneys to visit their client, although she was able to speak with him briefly Tuesday.
Parra-Hernandez remains in ICE custody while receiving hospital treatment.
Parra-Hernandez’s brother, Rodolfo Parra, also spoke Wednesday, pleading with authorities to allow Miguel to remain in the hospital.
“Le pedimos a todas las autoridades con poder que nos ayuden a que no muevan a mi hermano del hospital porque se encuentra en un estado crítico y que nos apoyen en este caso para que se haga justicia,” Rodolfo said.
Translated into English, he asked authorities with the power to intervene to help keep his brother hospitalized because of his serious condition and to support the family’s pursuit of justice.
The family says its immediate priority is making sure Parra-Hernandez receives the medical treatment he needs.
Another issue raised Wednesday was the identity of the man ICE was reportedly trying to apprehend.
ICE has said its agents were conducting an operation targeting a driver with an active warrant when people fled and Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an agent’s vehicle.
His family and representatives dispute that account.
Espinosa identified the person ICE was reportedly seeking as José Mendoza Cervantes.
He said people FIEL has interviewed, including individuals connected to the incident, do not recognize that name.
During the news conference, Espinosa showed photographs and questioned family members about whether they recognized the individual.
Both Nidia and Rodolfo said they had never seen the man pictured.
Espinosa also displayed a photograph of a man he said was in the truck with Parra-Hernandez that morning, arguing that the individual did not match the person ICE was reportedly seeking.
FIEL questioned whether the operation was truly directed at a specific individual and raised concerns about possible racial profiling.
Those allegations have not been independently verified. The family’s inability to identify the person ICE reportedly sought does not establish whether that individual exists or whether agents had a valid target.
The new witness information follows serious allegations made by Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare about how the investigation was handled after the collision.
Teare said sheriff’s deputies had a tow truck ready to remove the ICE SUV so investigators could examine its crash data recorder.
According to Teare, ICE agents declined to consent to the download, prompting investigators to begin preparing a search warrant.
But before that warrant could be obtained, Teare said an ICE agent got back into the SUV and drove away.
Teare said driving the vehicle again may have erased information stored in its crash data recorder.
He has also said surveillance footage reviewed by his office and experienced crash investigators suggests Parra-Hernandez was struck intentionally.
That conclusion is disputed by ICE’s account of the incident, and no criminal charges have been announced.
The district attorney’s office is evaluating whether the circumstances could support an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon charge, a second-degree felony punishable by up to 20 years in prison.
NBC News has also reported that multiple ICE officers were wearing body cameras during the incident and that ICE is reviewing footage internally.
Teare has said his office has not been given access to that footage.
The Harris County District Attorney’s Office is continuing its criminal investigation and working to obtain statements from potential witnesses, including the men who were detained inside the ICE vehicle.
Bruno and FIEL are also seeking assurances that Parra-Hernandez will remain hospitalized long enough to receive his next surgery and necessary medical care.
Several questions remain unanswered, including what the detained witnesses actually saw, whether prosecutors will obtain the body-camera footage and vehicle data, and whether ICE intends to transfer Parra-Hernandez before he completes treatment.
KPRC 2 is seeking clarification from ICE and the Harris County Sheriff’s Office about the new claims raised Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Explained: Reforms to the IMF and World Bank's debt framework send a new climate signal – adaptation counts
articles.title_zh: Explained: Reforms to the IMF and World Bank's debt framework send a new climate signal – adaptation counts
articles.content_orig:
The leading framework assessing low-income countries’ economic health has enhanced its coverage of climate vulnerability and now rewards adaptation investments.
The recently concluded review by the IMF and World Bank of the low-income countries’ debt sustainability framework (LIC-DSF) makes important progress on adaptation. Changes to methodologies will now enhance the realism of debt outlooks to better reflect growing physical damages linked to climate change and incorporate benefits of proactive investments in adaptation and resilience. Following successive climate shocks, such as Nepal’s catastrophic glacier melt, the IMF and World Bank’s adjustments mark an important and welcomed step toward providing early warnings of climate vulnerability in economic frameworks and incentivising investment in resilience.
The debt sustainability framework (DSF) is the main tool for multilateral institutions and other creditors to assess risks to debt sustainability in low-income countries (LICs). Simply put, it captures a country’s economic health. Its forward-looking approach is designed to send early signals about borrowing capacity and strengthen resilience to shocks. Its results determine countries’ eligibility for grants and other concessional support. Official and private creditors, as well as other participants such as credit rating agencies, also use LIC-DSF results to inform their analysis of a country’s economic and financial health and, by extension, their lending terms.
Policy frameworks at the IMF and World Bank are periodically reviewed to maintain agility and effectiveness. The review of the LIC-DSF comes at a time of significant debt pressures worldwide and compounding risks, including physical shocks and geopolitical turmoil. 58 countries are already experiencing or at high risk of debt distress, and prolonged conflict in the Middle East could increase pressure .
At the same time, low-income countries are more vulnerable to rising climate impacts, with many facing a “ debt–climate nexus ” where debt pressures crowd out adaptation and resilience investments and physical shocks in turn worsen debt pressures.
Record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires in much of the Northern Hemisphere, the catastrophic glacier melts in Nepal, and a turbocharged El Niño in the equatorial Pacific are some of the latest examples of what a warming planet means for people and their livelihoods. In 2025 alone, direct economic losses from extreme weather events topped US$ 220 billion according to Swiss RE.

articles.title_orig: World News in Brief: Gaza braces for winter amid attacks, joint patrols in CAR, 90 cities commit to sustainable development
articles.title_zh: World News in Brief: Gaza braces for winter amid attacks, joint patrols in CAR, 90 cities commit to sustainable development
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
The UN and its partners are stepping up preparations in Gaza for the approaching cold and rainy season, even as attacks affecting civilians continue, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said on Wednesday.
Over the past two days, partners recorded multiple airstrikes, as well as shelling, demolition blasts, naval fire and shooting across all of Gaza’s governorates, particularly west of the so-called “yellow line” established by Israeli authorities.
Humanitarians brought in additional fuel, plastic tarpaulins, winter clothing, medicines and medical supplies, but OCHA said these limited items were insufficient to meet people’s needs. Deliveries remain constrained by underfunding and Israeli restrictions, including bans on some partners’ operations, limits on imports such as engine oil and spare parts and restricted access to more than 64 per cent of Gaza’s land.
Meanwhile, the UN human rights office in the Occupied Palestinian Territory condemned an Israeli raid on Tuesday on premises in Al Bira, Ramallah, which Israeli forces claimed were the offices of two Palestinian civil society organizations, Addameer and the Union of Palestinian Women’s Committee.
Soldiers confiscated files and equipment and detained a journalist and a former prisoner, the office said, calling for an immediate end to the crackdown on Palestinian civic space.
Humanitarian partners called on Israeli authorities to stop the crackdown on Palestinian civic space, noting that such raids and the detention of human rights defenders and protection workers have had a “chilling effect”.
UN peacekeepers and national troops in the Central African Republic are stepping up joint patrols in the Vakaga prefecture in response to security concerns, the UN peacekeeping mission in the country, MINUSCA , said on Wednesday.
On Monday afternoon, peacekeepers from MINUSCA’s Zambian contingent and Central African Armed Forces (FACA) personnel patrolled the main roads in and around Birao. Patrols are also being reinforced in Am-Dafock and several surrounding localities.
The aim is to prevent threats against civilians, reassure communities and build trust between security forces and residents amid concerns and circulating rumours about the security situation.
“These joint operations reassure us. They alleviate our worries regarding the rumours and information currently circulating in our prefecture,” said Ahamat Adam, a community leader and member of the local peace committee, who hopes the patrols will be extended to other localities, including Tiringoulou and Sikikéde.
The patrols are also helping daily life and the local economy.
“When we see the FACA and MINUSCA patrolling together in town, we feel safer. It allows us to carry out our daily activities with greater confidence,” said Amina Alit, a trader at the Birao market.
Ninety mayors from 50 countries met at the UN Forum of Mayors in Geneva earlier this week, renewing their commitments to make cities more sustainable and sending its recommendations to the UN Committee on Urban Development, Housing and Land Management , which opened its latest session on Wednesday.
Established in 2020, the Forum of Mayors connects city, national and global actors to share local solutions for implementing the UN Sustainable Development Goals .
Their commitments cover six areas:
The mayors noted that across all areas, fiscal constraints, fragmented governance and limited local capacity hinder implementation and urged States and international organizations to strengthen the legal, institutional, policy and financial frameworks needed to address the issue.
The head of the UN Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE), which organises the forum, explained why cities must be at the heart of decision-making.
“Cities are where people experience the major challenges of our time most directly – from housing and access to essential services to mobility, climate impacts, inequality and disaster risks. But, cities are also where solutions are being developed every day,” she said.

articles.title_orig: China will continue to play 'constructive' role for 'comprehensive' ceasefire in Middle East, says top diplomat
articles.title_zh: China will continue to play 'constructive' role for 'comprehensive' ceasefire in Middle East, says top diplomat
articles.content_orig:
Top Chinese diplomat Wang Yi said Wednesday that Beijing will play a "constructive" role in realizing a "comprehensive" ceasefire in the Middle East, and resume long-stalled negotiations between rival parties.
"We will uphold the series of initiatives and propositions put forward by President Xi (Jinping) dedicated to peace and stability, and continue to make China's contribution and play China's constructive role in realizing a comprehensive ceasefire in the Middle East, advancing political settlement, resuming negotiations at an early date, and achieving lasting peace," said Wang, according to the Foreign Ministry.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said in a post on the US social media company X that Wang made the remarks during a meeting with Khaldoon Khalifa Al Mubarak, special envoy of the President of the UAE to China, in Beijing.
Wang said that as the Middle East undergoes profound changes, conflicts are dragging on at multiple levels, and their spillover effects continue to weigh on regional security and development.
The path to peace has never been smooth, and promoting peace and ending conflicts requires pooling efforts, said Wang. "We believe that as long as all parties remain committed to the choice of peace and maintain the resolve for peace, a bright future for the Middle East will surely be realized."
China has always been a builder of peace, a promoter of stability and a contributor to development in the Middle East, he added.

articles.title_orig: At the table: The women who have shaped US-China trade policy
articles.title_zh: At the table: The women who have shaped US-China trade policy
articles.content_orig:
Four women have served as United States Trade Representative during pivotal moments in America’s economic relationship with China, collectively shaping U.S. trade policy across four administrations and four decades — from the opening bids of the early 1990s and China’s entry into the WTO, through the tariff wars, technology controls, and supply chain upheavals of the present day. They have sat across the table from Chinese counterparts through boom years and breakdown years alike, negotiating in moments when the relationship still ran on cautious optimism and in moments when it had hardened into strategic rivalry. They have never shared a stage together – until now. They are:
On December 3 from 10:45 to 12:00 pm, they will reflect candidly on the deals they closed, the moments that didn’t go as planned, and the decisions they might revisit with the benefit of hindsight. They will also turn to the present and the future: what today’s policymakers should learn from four decades of engagement and estrangement, and what choices now confront the United States as it navigates its most consequential and complicated bilateral economic relationship.
Ambassador Charlene Barshefsky is Chair of Parkside Global Advisors and former United States Trade Representative. She served as U.S. Trade Representative from 1997 to 2001 and as Acting and Deputy USTR from 1993 to 1996. As a member of President Bill Clinton’s Cabinet, Barshefsky was responsible for shaping U.S. trade policy and negotiating hundreds of trade, market access, and investment agreements around the world. She is particularly known as the architect and chief U.S. negotiator of the landmark agreement that paved the way for China’s accession to the World Trade Organization, as well as for negotiations involving financial services, telecommunications, high-technology products, and intellectual property. Barshefsky previously served as Senior International Partner at WilmerHale and currently chairs the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations. She also serves on several corporate and nonprofit boards and is a member of the Council on Foreign Relations.
Ambassador Carla A. Hills is a Senior Counselor at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group and a distinguished leader in U.S. trade policy and international economic affairs. She served as United States Trade Representative from 1989 to 1993 under President George H.W. Bush, acting as the President’s principal adviser on international trade policy and chief U.S. trade negotiator. During her tenure, Hills negotiated and concluded the North American Free Trade Agreement and led U.S. negotiations in the Uruguay Round, which helped lay the foundation for the World Trade Organization. Earlier in her career, she served as Secretary of Housing and Urban Development under President Gerald Ford and as Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Division of the Department of Justice. Hills is Chair Emeritus of the Council on Foreign Relations and Honorary Chair of the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations and the Inter-American Dialogue. She earned her B.A. from Stanford University and J.D. from Yale Law School.
Ambassador Susan C. Schwab is Professor Emerita at the University of Maryland School of Public Policy, Strategic Advisor in Mayer Brown’s International Trade practice, and Chair of the Board of Directors of the National Foreign Trade Council. She served as United States Trade Representative from 2006 to 2009 and as Deputy USTR from 2005 to 2006 under President George W. Bush. As USTR, Schwab concluded free trade agreements with Peru, Colombia, and South Korea, launched the initial Trans-Pacific Partnership negotiations, participated in the WTO Doha Round, and pursued or resolved major trade disputes involving China, Canada, and the European Union. Her career has also included service as Dean of the University of Maryland School of Public Policy, Assistant Secretary of Commerce and Director General of the U.S. & Foreign Commercial Service, and Director of Corporate Business Development at Motorola, where she worked on business negotiations in China and elsewhere in Asia.
Ambassador Katherine Tai is Executive Director and Co-Founder of the Coalition for New Trade and served as the 19th United States Trade Representative from 2021 to 2025. As a member of President Joe Biden’s Cabinet, she was the administration’s principal trade adviser, negotiator, and spokesperson and led the development of its worker-centered approach to trade policy. Before her unanimous Senate confirmation as USTR, Tai served as Chief Trade Counsel and Trade Subcommittee Staff Director for the House Ways and Means Committee, where she played a central role in negotiations surrounding the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. Earlier, she served at USTR as a WTO litigator and later as Chief Counsel for China Trade Enforcement. Tai began her career in private legal practice and also taught English in Guangzhou, China, as a Yale-China Association fellow. She holds a B.A. in history from Yale University and a J.D. from Harvard Law School and is fluent in Mandarin.
Ambassador Jon M. Huntsman, Jr. is Vice Chairman and President of Strategic Growth at Mastercard, where he leads work on partnerships with governments and public-sector institutions as well as the company’s inclusive growth, philanthropy, and sustainability initiatives. Huntsman has held senior public-service roles under both Republican and Democratic administrations, serving as U.S. Ambassador to Singapore, China, and Russia. He is the only American to have served as chief of mission in both China and Russia. Huntsman also served as Deputy United States Trade Representative, negotiating trade and investment agreements across Asia and Africa, and was twice elected Governor of Utah. Earlier in his career, he held senior positions in the U.S. Department of Commerce and the private sector. He currently serves on the boards of Ford Motor Company and Chevron and is a trustee of the Huntsman Foundation. Huntsman is a graduate of the University of Pennsylvania.

articles.title_orig: Golden State Valkyries hit record $100 million annual revenue as world's most valuable women's sports franchise nearing $1 billion
articles.title_zh: Golden State Valkyries hit record $100 million annual revenue as world's most valuable women's sports franchise nearing $1 billion
articles.content_orig:
SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- The Golden State Valkyries have become the first professional women's sports team to generate $100 million in annual revenue, adding another milestone to a season that has drawn sold-out crowds and helped make the franchise the most valuable team in not just the WNBA, but across all of women's sports.
The Valkyries will face the Atlanta Dream in the WNBA Finals, with Game 1 scheduled for 12:30 p.m. Saturday at Chase Center, where fans have packed the arena throughout the season.
Among them is Jennifer Ling of Foster City, a season-ticket holder who said she has spent heavily supporting the team.
"My wallet doesn't love me right now. I came here to get some finals merch," Ling said.
Ling said she has spent more than $1,000 on the team over the past two years.
MORE: WNBA Finals Games 3, 4 in Atlanta move to State Farm Arena to accommodate more fans
A supporter since the franchise's launch, Ling said, "I was really stoked to be a part of something special."
Fans say the Valkyries' success extends beyond the court.
"I have an 8-year-old daughter. To see her excitement around this is awesome," fan Dalan McNabola said.
The team's business performance has also drawn attention. This year, the Valkyries became the first professional women's sports team to generate $100 million in annual revenue. According to Sportico , the franchise is valued at $850 million, an astonishing number in just their second year that puts them at the top of all women's sports teams.
"It is super exciting, especially for an expansion team to do this in year two is incredible," McNabola said.
Sports columnist Bruce Jenkins said the Valkyries have become a model for the league and for women's sports more broadly.
"This is what the WNBA has always wanted to be and it is right here. And they are setting the standard," Jenkins said.
Nola Agha, a professor of sport management at the University of San Francisco, said the franchise's success is rooted in strong leadership and execution.
"They have an amazing ownership group and they have an amazing president who know how to monetize and who know how to run a really professional franchise," Agha said.
"They're hiring great coaches, great players, and they know how to win," she added.
Agha also credited the team's devoted fan base.
"This team is tapping into a fan base that's never had the opportunity to purchase tickets to an exciting game, to an exciting product," Agha said. "There's lots of excited fans in women's basketball."
With sold-out crowds at Chase Center, the Valkyries continue to draw enthusiastic support as they prepare for the WNBA FInals.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says SpaceX hampers drones for attack and defence, as US ties fray
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says SpaceX hampers drones for attack and defence, as US ties fray
articles.content_orig:
Launch of Russian ballistic missiles on Ukraine, with no US warning, coincides with outage of Starlink managed by Musk’s SpaceX
Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.
The terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the terminals travelling at high speeds on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Donald Trump has denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine . Zelenskyy also indicated that the US was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine in an interview with NPR aired on Wednesday, but confirmed that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited.
Ukraine did not receive any warning before Russia launched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening, according to Col Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the air force. But it did receive warnings from “foreign partners” about three subsequent barrages, leaving further confusion about whether or not the US is intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine.
Musk said that Starlink is not licensed to clients who are using weapons, and that the Ukrainian military was linked to a separate network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government. “This is not under SpaceX control,” Musk wrote.
Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.
“With their actions our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.
But there have been no reports that access for static Starlink terminals has been cut, meaning critical battlefield communications for soldiers should remain unaffected. The detection of incoming Russian missiles and drones relies on other technologies.
Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader – an extraordinary act of political interference against a wartime ally – as a personal feud between the two presidents has burst into the open.
The reports that Starlink was being throttled on the frontlines were interpreted by some as further pressure on Ukraine to end the fighting and make a deal with Russia at any cost.
Serhii Sternenko, a political activist with close ties to the military, first reported the outage and later said that the speeds at which the loss of connectivity occurred had fallen even lower. “It is likely that the company ‘SpaceX’ resorted to such measures at the request of the Trump administration,” he said. “Ordinary satellite communication terminals are currently operational.”
after newsletter promotion
Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
Zelenskyy had suggested, though not said, that the US was intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine about impending Russian missile strikes.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” Zelenskyy said. “Russia does not consider the American president’s statements strong.”
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become even more widespread.
Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed by either side. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”
Ukraine is observing a short-term moratorium on striking Russian refineries while Kyiv seeks to show that it is ready for talks with Russia. Zelenskyy arrived in London on Wednesday to meet Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister. He will also be received by King Charles.
Zelenskyy is seeking new negotiations with the US. He has sent proposals to the Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, saying Ukraine was ready to work towards a ceasefire and “Russia must also be part of this agreement”.

articles.title_orig: Archery: a living tradition at the World Nomad Games
articles.title_zh: Archery: a living tradition at the World Nomad Games
articles.content_orig:
At the beginning of September 2026, the world’s most unique multi-sport event took place in Kyrgyzstan in Central Asia. The biennial World Nomad Games attracts traditional sports athletes from nomadic and non-nomadic cultures alike – with a traditional archery competition at the heart of it.
This year, Kyrgyzstan played host for the fourth time. More than 3,000 athletes and delegates from 106 countries participated across 40 sport disciplines, spread across nine different locations. Beginning in 2014 as a gathering of 19 countries, a grand ambition has long been part of it, both as as a unifying project for the region and a projection of soft power.
The Games’ most famous and eye-catching event is kok-buru , a ferocious equestrian sport played with a goat carcass, but archery has long been a part of the nomadic cultures celebrated and was prominent in the buildup.
By far the most visible part of the competition worldwide was was the spectacular opening ceremony, held in a brand new arena in the capital Bishkek, featuring hundreds of horses ridden in formation and seen on countless social media feeds around the world.
I was part of the six-strong archery delegation from Great Britain – not a nation known for modern nomadism, but who sent just under fifty athletes across a dozen sports, with experience in each ranging from more than a decade to just a few weeks.
In traditional archery, over 250 archers from 51 countries would take part across the three days of competition. The rules required you to use the traditional bow of your country – which across Great Britain is the English longbow – and also require wooden arrows and feather fletchings with wooden nocks, although modern strings are permitted. Arrows must be shot off the hand; no shelves or rests are permitted.
The GBR team, gathered by the UK Traditional Archers' International Association, were the only athletes shooting longbows, with all other nations adopting some variety of Asiatic bow. Transporting two-metre-long one-piece wooden bows safely across the world to the shooting line was just one of the many challenges to solve.
A further rule was that you must wear the traditional national dress of your country when shooting – which is difficult, because the United Kingdom doesn't have one. With several of the team having Celtic heritage, we brewed up a concept designed to reflect and blend English, Scottish, Welsh, and Irish lineages and cultures, while still being practical to shoot in (the photo shows some of the team with the British ambassador).
The archery events were held in the extraordinary arena of the Kyrchyn Gorge, a pasture halfway up the towering mountain range that divides Kyrgyzstan from its neighbour Kazakhstan, with snow-capped ridges brooding above surrounded by swirling fog.
It's fair to say that it was a different experience from most archery competitions. The area hosted sports ranging from arm wrestling to bird hunting and even Kyrgyz sighthound racing, with weather apt to change five times in a day and precious little shelter.
The rugged nature of the location was a challenge in itself: my seat on the bus to the gorge found me sitting next to a live golden eagle, while one way in on foot required you to ford streams over stepping stones.
An enormous bazaar with a living exhibition called 'Universe Of Nomads' next door attracted tens of thousands of tourists from near and far, and the constant crowds, noise, music and woodsmoke sometimes gave the event the feel of a free festival rather than a sporting competition. You hadn't put your bow down for a minute before an enterprising local trotted up to offer you a horseback ride.
Things happened when they happened, nomad style. It was a extraordinary set of experiences, but one that required patience and endurance.
While a big part of the experience was the cultural exchange across nations, the competition was serious with some of the world's most experienced traditional archers taking part.
The three days reflected three different national traditions: Kyrgyz, Turkish, and Korean. The first day saw competition at the Kyrgyz 'Teke Buta' target shot at 40 metres, shooting nine ends of seven arrows each at an unfamiliar face featuring five scoring rings encircled by a devious mountain goat.
What made it even harder was the positional requirements; three ends were shot standing as normal, three from a reversed stance – a kind of standing Parthian shot, where our hips faced away from the target – and three ends kneeling, with knee pads provided. (I’d practised this as best I could, but it is particularly difficult with a full-length longbow.)
The Turkish 'Puta' event saw women shooting at 60 metres and men at 70 metres with a uniquely shaped hit-or-miss target, familiar to viewers of the Conquest Cup .
Finally the last day of competition saw Korean traditional competition on a massive 145 metre range at traditional Korean targets , held in almost continuous heavy rain which soaked the arrows, fletchings and archers – and made a difficult task with a longbow almost impossible. A very cold and damp set of archers left the field for the final time.
The archers participating reflected a huge variety of interests and heritage. The Australian archery delegation included Merjem Colan, who trains at the Maydaan Archery Club in Sydney, a unique club which promotes Islamic Ottoman archery heritage in the city.
Merjem and her team were some of the highest placed Western athletes in competition. “We practice Ottoman archery as more than a sport, we connect the technical skill with our history, character and community. While Australia’s traditional archery scene is spread across different organisations, that diversity gives people many ways to enter through culture, competition and craftsmanship,” she said.
“We trained through traditional Ottoman methodology, using repetition and foundational practices like kepaze and torba to develop consistency, precision and composure under pressure. But our training also develops the whole person, the internal alongside the external through discipline, patience, humility and good character,” added Merjem.
What was the most interesting part for you? “The most interesting aspect of the competition was definitely the nomadic culture. Seeing the landscape of Kyrchyn Gorge, it became clear why the nomadic tradition survives for so long in those mountains. It was beautiful to see the continuation and passing down of many of the skills from one generation to the next. Especially for me, I was amazed by the textile traditions and of course, horseback riding!”
The international traditional archery scene is governed by the World Traditional Archery Federation , who oversee an annual World Cup among much else. It maintains a living tradition that connects us not just to history, but to a dedicated global community of practitioners.
Indeed, the true value of the World Nomad Games was the vibrant celebration of shared human heritage, and we found ourselves warmly welcomed into the global nomadic tribe.
The next World Nomad Games will be held in Kazan in 2028.
Some photos courtesy Pablo Ruiz-Múzquiz

articles.title_orig: RINK TO WRENCHES: Noah West’s Journey Through Childhood in Racing, Professional Hockey, World of Outlaws Crew Chief
articles.title_zh: RINK TO WRENCHES: Noah West’s Journey Through Childhood in Racing, Professional Hockey, World of Outlaws Crew Chief
articles.content_orig:
October 14, 2026 at 2:10 pm
Dirt Sprint Car racing always occupied a space in Noah West’s mind no matter where life took him.
How could it not, after growing up in an environment that brought the likes of Jimmy Carr, Steve “Scuba” Swenson, Sonny Kreitzer, and others around him?
West was born in New York right into a racing family and moved to a major motorsports hub during his formative years.
“It’s kind of been something that we’ve always been involved in,” West said. “That’s why we actually moved out here to Indy. My dad (Jeff West) started Supermodified racing out in the northeast up in Oswego, building his own cars, chassis, stuff like that. Then he actually moved to Indy to work for Eddie Cheever in IndyCar doing some repair work and carbon repair stuff. From there, he started his own business with IPC.”
His father’s business introduced him to the famed crew chiefs previously mentioned. It’s also the time when he began to learn the mechanical basics of race cars. Lessons learned from his dad and other key figures would eventually lead West to wrenching for his own family’s World of Outlaws NOS Energy Drink Sprint Car operation.
“My dad obviously taught me a lot of what I know from the mechanical side of things,” West said. “I spent a lot of time with Brinton Marvel and his dad Justin and was kind of just always learning as well with Ayrton (Olsen) and his dad. I was always surrounded by some really good minds in the sport.”
West’s teenage years brought a new passion outside of racing: hockey. The same competitive drive that fueled his family’s racing endeavors helped West reach Big Ten Conference level collegiate competition at the University of Michigan before a season of professional play in the ECHL with the Kansas City Mavericks.
“I raced Go-Karts when I was growing up, but hockey took over,” West recalled. “It just consumes your life, the same as Sprint Car racing. If you’re not eating, breathing, and sleeping hockey, you’re not going to be successful at it and be able to do it at the level we’re trying to do it at. Hockey, yeah, it’s a winter sport, but it’s really year-round. You’re training day in and day out six days a week, sometimes seven depending on the time of year. So, it consumed a ton of time and was a blast.”
Hockey may have required most of his time, but his love for racing never wavered. West remained involved in his family’s team, Three Stooges Racing, and their primarily pavement race cars. West truly began to lean into the dirt when the opportunity arose to turn the wrenches on the Hayward Motorsports No. 19 in 2023. That combination started strong as C.J. Leary put the car in the Eldora Million and finished 12th.
As West continued to lead the Hayward crew, the hunger to launch his own Sprint Car operation grew. He periodically attempted to persuade his father until finally he was convinced to add a dirt Winged Sprint Car to the Three Stooges stable.
“It was always something I really wanted to do,” West said of going Winged Sprint Car racing on dirt. “I mean, the pavement cars were fun, but I always told dad, ‘We need to have a Winged Sprint Car. Let’s go Winged Sprint Car racing.’ And it was always, ‘Well, when you’re out of college, we’ll start putting that together.’ Sure enough, my last year of college, the deal with Brodie (Hayward) was kind of ending, and I told my dad, ‘This is what I want to do still. We’re getting close to that time. Let’s do something.’ That was right after Kings Royal that year. I think we sat in the shop and talked and said let’s do it. He drove 10 minutes home to the house, and by the time I got home he called me and said, ‘Well, I got two cars on the way, and we’ll start this and put it together and see what we can do.’” The Three Stooges Racing No. 51 debuted just over a year ago and is now winding down its first season on the World of Outlaws tour (Tyler Carr Photo)
The Three Stooges Racing No. 51 Sprint Car debuted during the 2025 Kings Royal week with Joel Myers Jr. in the seat. Eventually, Scott Bogucki came aboard to close out the year with a pick-and-choose schedule as a plan began to form for them to go World of Outlaws racing in 2026.
“My dad was driving somewhere with my mom, probably leaving a brother’s hockey game or something; he called me and said, ‘I think we should just go Outlaw racing,’” West said. “I was like, ‘If that’s what you want to do, we’ll do it.’ He did some more talking to some people that we know and got everything together.”
They began the season with Bogucki and picked up a podium at only the eighth race of the campaign when he drove from ninth to second at Lawton Speedway . The two sides parted ways in May before the team brought Ashton Torgerson aboard for most of the summer. Then came their current pilot, Steven Snyder Jr., with his first weekend in the car at the Ironman 55 in early August.
West believes he and the 20-year-old out of Rising Sun, MD are gelling fast and laying the foundations of a potent partnership. The results agree. Snyder Jr. drove from 16th to sixth at the Front Row Challenge during just their fourth night together. Less than a month later, he led laps before a top-five finish at Huset’s Speedway. Then came a 10th-to-second charge at El Paso County Raceway for Snyder’s first World of Outlaws podium. He battled for a win at Ventura Raceway to close out September.
“Steven, he’s got very high upside and potential,” West said. “We both want to build together and work together. We’re both ultra-competitive. Will it bite us some nights? Yes, but at the end of the day if I’m out here giving 110%, the last thing I want is for my driver who’s getting in my race car to not give me 110% back. I feel like with Steven here these last three months, he’s came in and given us that. As a crew chief and car owner, that’s all we can ask for.” Noah West and Steven Snyder Jr. have proven they’re connecting quickly during the latter half of 2026 (Tyler Carr Photo)
The short-term future with Snyder isn’t all that’s on West’s mind as they continue to grow. This isn’t merely some quick experiment. West wants to construct an organization to contend with the best of the best for years to come. He knows he may not always be able to be the one going up and down the road with the team, but he’s putting the pieces in place for his team to do so and continue the family racing tradition he was born into.
“I’d like to establish it into something like Big Game and what Tod Quiring has built there and KCP (Racing), Roth (Motorsports). I want to establish us to be something like that,” West said. “Whether it’s myself out here on the road full-time for years to come, I don’t know. I want to keep doing it, and I want to be out here for a few more years, but I’d like to turn it into something where when it’s time to have a family and kids and stuff I can also be at home while our team will be out here competing with the World of Outlaws.”
West, Snyder Jr., and the Three Stooges Racing crew continue to wind down the 2026 season this weekend at Indiana’s Lincoln Park Speedway on Friday, Oct. 16, and Illinois’ Belle-Clair Fairgrounds Park Speedway on Saturday, Oct. 17. For tickets, CLICK HERE .

articles.title_orig: Is it time for China to rethink its Houthi policy?
articles.title_zh: Is it time for China to rethink its Houthi policy?
articles.content_orig:
Walking a tightrope between Riyadh and Tehran, Beijing has little room to manoeuvre, but it is not without options. More air defence systems and drones could help defend Saudi Arabia
Is it time for China to rethink its Houthi policy?
Earlier this month, the Yemen-based Houthi militia turned their Iranian-sponsored weapons on Saudi Arabia in the most horrific way, targeting not military or economic infrastructure, but civilians at an airport. The missiles hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over several days, killing 20 and injuring over 370. Additional attacks on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam were intercepted.
Since the Saudi-Houthi conflict reignited in recent weeks, the group has also struck oil facilities, inflicting casualties and causing significant damage. Military analysts note a marked increase in the Houthis’ targeting accuracy. Clearly, neither they nor their backer have been idle since the 2022 ceasefire, building up a drone and missile stockpile despite the UN-mandated arms embargo and Saudi-led blockade.
Missiles have been flying since the US-Israeli war against Iran that began on 28 February led Iran and its proxies (including groups in Iraq) to hit back against America’s Gulf allies. For Beijing, the attacks against Saudi oil infrastructure are an unwelcome development. Saudi Arabia is China’s second-largest oil supplier, accounting for 14% of its total crude imports, so this will squeeze China’s oil supply and, by extension, harm its economy.
True to form, it condemned the attacks while calling for restraint, de-escalation, and a return to the negotiating table (Beijing’s standard response to Middle Eastern conflicts). Yet the stakes are now much higher. Some think the time may have come for Beijing to offer more substantive help to Saudi Arabia.
Following the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and the subsequent ‘closure’ of the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia used its East-West pipeline to export more than 70% of its pre-war total crude exports via the Red Sea, bypassing Hormuz and the Iranian threat, but most of this re-routed oil then passed Yemen, through the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the Gulf of Aden, before heading to East Asian customers like China. This kept global oil prices high but tolerable, so China did not need to exhaust its oil reserves.
Since September, however, the situation has changed. The Houthis advanced down Yemen’s west coast to wrest control of Bab al-Mandab from the Saudi-backed government of Yemen (currently based in Aden) while Iran’s Iraq-based militias attacked the Saudi East-West Pipeline.
Although the US has disabled enough Iranian radars to make it possible for ships to transit the Strait of Hormuz under US naval escort, the route remains perilous. Meanwhile, the Suez Canal is off-limits to fully-laden very large crude carriers, forcing Saudi oil tankers to take the longer, more costly journey around Africa to reach their customers in East Asia. As a result, global oil prices have soared in recent days, surpassing $100 per barrel.
Sinopec storage tanks are seen at the crude oil refinery Sinopec Jinling Petrochemical Plant in Nanjing, in China's eastern Jiangsu province on 8 May 2026.
Until now, China had largely been insulated from the fallout, with its vast oil stockpile and Russian crude imports continuing, but Ukrainian attacks against Russian oil refineries has changed the picture, with China suspending diesel, gasoline, and jet fuel exports this October.
The Houthi attacks risk straining China-Saudi relations. Beijing would like to be on good terms with both the Arab countries and Iran, but since the US-Israeli war against Iran began in February, this balancing act has become increasingly difficult. Iran’s attack on Arab countries and its closure of the Strait of Hormuz have increased tensions dramatically, leading Beijing to postpone the upcoming China-Arab States Summit indefinitely.

Your newsletter subscriptions are subject to Al Majalla privacy

Beijing would like to be on good terms with both the Arab countries and Iran, but the US war on Iran has made this balancing act increasingly difficult
China's habit of keeping Middle Eastern conflicts at arm's length is nothing new. Saudi Arabia is aware that its ties to China are largely economic, so it knows that Beijing will condemn Iranian attacks but offer little else. If Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia continue, however, Riyadh may expect more from China, at which point Beijing could no longer sit on the sidelines, given that Saudi Arabia is one of China's most important Middle Eastern partners.
Following an appeal from Riyadh in September, China asked Iran to rein in the Houthis. On 12 October, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi offered to mediate talks between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. Yet having captured the port of Mokha and placed the strategic city of Taiz under siege, the Houthis have the upper hand and are unlikely to negotiate in good faith.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting in Beijing, China, on 2 September 2025.
What (if anything) should China do to defend its Saudi partner? Although it has long adhered to the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence (put forward by Chinese premier Zhou Enlai in 1953), China has never signed a defence pact with Saudi Arabia, given its ties with Iran, which also supplies China with oil. This effectively rules out direct Chinese military action against the Houthis. Yet it does not rule out China giving Saudi Arabia Chinese-made air-defence systems, which Gulf states already deploy. Beijing could also give Saudi Arabia more drones.
Interceptors (even those made in China) are expensive, and it can take several to bring down a projectile. Even for a wealthy country like Saudi Arabia, this is unsustainable in the long term, when Houthi drones and missiles cost a fraction of the amount. Armed drones, by contrast, are far more cost-effective. They could hit Houthi military targets, loiter over Houthi-occupied territory, and suppress enemy fire. They do not replace interceptors, but they would give Riyadh a cheaper, more effective first line of defence.
Walking a tightrope between Riyadh and Tehran, Beijing has little room to manoeuvre, but it is not without options. More air defence systems and drones could help defend Saudi Arabia without crossing any red lines. Whether it will act, however, is another matter. For now, the rope holds, but it will not hold forever.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX rocket launch causes stunning ‘jellyfish cloud’ visible off US east coast
articles.title_zh: SpaceX rocket launch causes stunning ‘jellyfish cloud’ visible off US east coast
articles.content_orig:
Expanding plume of fuel exhaust crystalized in the sky and reflected sunlight off frozen particles after Florida launch
A SpaceX rocket provided a stunning pre-dawn display over Florida as a egiant, luminescent “jellyfish cloud” spread for miles, caused by an expanding plume of fuel exhaust crystalizing in the sky and reflecting sunlight off the frozen particles.
The phenomenon occurred shortly after Tuesday’s 6.33am ET launch of the Falcon 9 rocket carrying cargo to the International Space Station.
The timing of the blastoff, 48 minutes before sunrise at Florida’s Cape Canaveral space force station, provided a perfect example of the colorful effect only fully visible from Earth during dusk and dawn launches.
The rocket’s north-eastern trajectory over the Atlantic also allowed residents of eastern states from Georgia to New York to enjoy the spectacle.
Nasa posted photographs of the jellyfish cloud on X , the social media platform owned by the SpaceX chief executive, Elon Musk. Among the hundreds of replies were images taken by sky watchers across multiple states.
Those who missed Tuesday’s dazzling celestial show have another opportunity to view one next Monday, 19 October, when another SpaceX Falcon 9 is scheduled to lift off from the same space force station pad.
An hour-long launch window for the satellite-deployment mission opens at 6.30am ET, little more than a half-hour before the 7.01am sunrise.

articles.title_orig: Stanford discovers way to save ghostly corals from the brink
articles.title_zh: Stanford discovers way to save ghostly corals from the brink
articles.content_orig:
Researchers at Stanford University have seen for the first time starving, struggling corals return to colorful, vibrant life within a matter of weeks by being placed in contact with healthy clones, genetically identical copies.
“This was shocking, stunning,” said Danny Collins, lead author of a study published Monday . “We were blown away [to] actually watch the healthy coral restore the color of the bleached corals essentially right before our eyes.”
Color returned within days, with full recovery occurring in just seven weeks — the fastest documented recovery to date.
“It was so much faster and more intense than we ever expected,” said Collins, a Ph.D. student at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability .
The results, seen in aquarium-sourced corals in a laboratory setting at the Hopkins Marine Station in Monterey County, could lead to faster and more complete recovery for wild corals suffering bleaching.
When ocean waters warm too fast, corals — a type of animal known to researchers as “cnidarians” — kick out helpful algae that live within their cells. This can kill the coral. Bleaching intensifies as the planet warms, threatening reefs around the globe. Reefs are critical habitats, making up just 0.01% of the ocean floor; they support a quarter of all marine life . They help economies thrive and protect against flooding and coastal erosion. The Coral Reef Alliance predicts within the next 30 years that 90% of reefs will experience severe annual bleaching.
The exciting thing about this work, Collins said, “is the demonstration that these bleached corals are not a lost cause, but actually have a remarkable potential to be recovered.”
Researchers knew that corals could become sick by touching objects holding dangerous bacteria. Last year, Collins looked at how corals catch disease when plastic waste settles on them. The plastic can harbor disease-causing bacteria and infect the coral.
“We were curious if we could harness that mechanism of contact, but instead of introducing bad guys that could cause disease, we could introduce good guys,” Collins said, “such as these beneficial algae that [healthy] corals harbor.”
Around the same time, Steve Palumbi, a professor in marine sciences at Stanford and study coauthor, saw in his lab that a sample colony had tipped over in a tank so that a healthy coral and a bleached one were touching each other. Where they touched, color returned to the sick coral.
So they tested it with other samples and were delighted with the results. The corals fused together, creating a nutrient bridge made of tissue, allowing the healthy individual to send over the life-giving, helpful algae.
“And within just a few weeks you get complete recovery,” Collins said.
They found the corals did not need to touch the entire time; just a brief period was needed, and the sick coral could quickly take it from there.
Creating genetic coral clones and placing them in contact with bleached twins isn’t a feasible recovery route for wild coral; it would take too much work to create a genetically identical, healthy copy of every coral in advance of a bleaching event. But the research does point the way forward for other restoration approaches.
“The key finding is that these bleached corals have remarkable capacity for rapid recovery that was not fully appreciated,” Collins said. “And that if you can get healthy algae into those bleached coral by any means necessary, they can recover at incredible rates.”
Scientists have documented bleached corals recovering in the field. But the process can take years, and many corals never recover or never recover fully. He’s excited to try a new avenue that is unexplored: “We hope these inspire a new set of interventions for coral reef restoration for recovering bleached corals.”
He and colleagues are now at work finding ways to extract algae, replicate them in a lab, and spread them to bleached corals. He hopes to test the method at field sites in Hawaii and Palau in the coming months to years.

articles.title_zh: SK Hynix Sinks 5% as China’s CXMT Aims at Server Memory; Western Digital Drops 4%, Micron Falls 3%
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SK Hynix fell 5% and Micron dropped 3% as China's CXMT targets server memory, the highest-margin segment driving AI chip profits.
The Roundhill Memory ETF dropped 4% while QQQ fell just 2%, confirming the selloff is tightly concentrated in memory names.

SK Hynix ( NASDAQ:SKHY ) stock is down 5% to $148.70 as China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) signals it's aiming a denser chip design at server memory. That push targets the most profitable corner of the memory market, and the selling is spreading across U.S.-listed names tied to AI data center buildouts. Memory and storage companies have delivered strong recent earnings, which puts pricing power at the center of the debate.
Meanwhile, Western Digital ( NASDAQ:WDC ) stock is down 4% to $364.04, a smaller drop than SK Hynix stock. Additionally, Micron Technology ( NASDAQ:MU ) stock is down 3% to $925.45, though it's still up 223% year to date.
Selling is concentrated in the memory/storage segment. The Roundhill Memory ETF ( CBOE:DRAM ) is down 4%, and its latest fact sheet shows SK Hynix at 24.2% and Micron at 23.8% of the fund. By comparison, a broader tech fund, the Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) is down just 2%.
Memory makers began selling off on October 12 after CXMT disclosed progress on a denser chip design. The slide has continued as CXMT points that capability at server memory, the highest-margin end of the market. SK Hynix stock has fallen 22% over the past month.

Its Q2 FY2026 preliminary revenue reached 79.32 trillion Korean won, up 256.8% year over year (YoY), with operating profit of 60.54 trillion won. A serious Chinese entrant threatens the premium pricing behind those gains.
SK Hynix and Micron make the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) that sits beside AI accelerators, putting CXMT's server push directly in their territory. Western Digital has operated as a pure-play hard disk drive (HDD) company since separating its flash business in February 2025, leaving it a step removed.
Micron's own results show how tight server memory remains. In fiscal Q4 2026, the company's revenue reached $54.23 billion, up 379.3% YoY, with a non-GAAP gross margin of 87%. The company guided fiscal Q1 2027 revenue to $61.5 billion.
On the September 30 earnings call, CEO Sanjay Mehrotra stated, "As we noted, in calendar year 27 as well as 2028, we see demand exceeding supply. In fact, we see greater tightness in the industry in 27 and in 28 versus 26." More than 75% of Micron's 2027 output is already committed, and Micron has signed 26 Strategic Customer Agreements carrying take-or-pay volumes. The call made no direct reference to CXMT.
Western Digital's latest quarter points to storage demand running on its own track. Its fiscal Q4 2026 revenue came in at $3.75 billion, up 43.8% YoY, while its non-GAAP gross margin expanded to 54.4%. CEO Irving Tan stated that "roughly 80% of data stored in a hyperscale data center resides on hard disk drives," adding that the pattern is likely to continue.
The next test for SK Hynix is whether CXMT can get its server memory qualified by hyperscale customers, as HSBC reaffirmed the stock as a top chip pick earlier this year with HBM leadership central to that bull case.
Micron's open variable is pricing on the 2027 output it has already committed. Management expects supply to stay tighter in calendar 2027 and 2028 than in 2026, so any hyperscaler shift toward CXMT would test that view.
Western Digital's fiscal Q1 2027 results, guided to $4.1 billion in revenue, could show whether hyperscale storage demand remains protected from memory pricing. Position sizes should be kept small until CXMT's server memory reaches customers.

articles.title_orig: The 10 Best Cities in the World for 2026, Ranked
articles.title_zh: The 10 Best Cities in the World for 2026, Ranked
articles.content_orig:
The word "best" is subjective, yet in moments of collective appreciation, people can agree on how special something is, like a book, a park, or a city.Â
One person may favor a city for its green space, tree-lined streets, and flowers blooming around bus stops, while another, with little interest in nature, might see these same features as unimportant.
Similarly, some travelers are fascinated by cities with many historical landmarks, hoping to uncover the stories of the past. Others, opposed to waiting in long lines, cross those destinations off their bucket lists for the same reason.
Some are easier to please, content with a sunny day, a cup of coffee, and a view! If you've ever been so captivated by a place that it becomes a feeling, you know what we're talking about.Â
While personal preferences ultimately write unique definitions of the "best" cities in the world, Oxford Economics outlined a few general categories to create a list.
The best cities in the world, though different in their own right, share one major quality: they offer locals and visitors a positive experience, whether living there or spending a week immersed in the culture before heading to the next destination.
These metropolises score highly in economics, human capital, quality of life, environment, and governance. Some cities received better scores in governance, others in economics, but the overall ranking combines all five categories.
For example, Copenhagen ranks number one for governance but doesn't make it into the top 10 for quality of life. Canberra leads in quality of life but isnât included on the list of cities with the strongest economies.
So which cities made the top 10 overall?
At number one is New York City , a choice many residents would shout from the rooftops. The Big Apple showcases historic landmarks, legendary sports teams, fashion-forward style, a stunning skyline, picturesque parks, bridges, museums, and more. Its much-welcomed diversity and seemingly endless career opportunities are hard to beat. And donât even get us started on the bagels, pizza, and sandwiches, or really anything âNew York styleâ for that matter. Travelers flock to the Statue of Liberty, the MET, Times Square, and Central Park, only to fall in love with the city's undeniable charm found on every street corner.
Second place goes to London , renowned for its royal history, timeless landmarks, beautiful parks, double-decker buses, afternoon tea traditions, and its influence on music and pop culture. Home to some of the worldâs most popular museums, vibrant neighborhoods, and a tidy transit system, London captivates visitors from around the world, inviting them to see Big Ben, ride the London Eye, and explore the city's historic castles and bridges.
Third is Paris , the City of Love, admired for its romantic atmosphere and famous attractions: the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre, Notre Dame Cathedral, cafes serving the worldâs best croissants and baguettes, effortless style, and a history written by revolution. Many only dream of walking along the Seine, popping in and out of shops on the Champs-ÃlysÃ©es, and biting into a perfect Parisian pastry.
Rounding out the top 10 are Seattle, San Francisco, Dublin, Boston, San Jose, Tokyo, and Zurich.
