articles.title_orig: Trump says "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is "getting ready to begin"
articles.title_zh: Trump says "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is "getting ready to begin"
articles.content_orig:
President Trump said Wednesday that "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration is preparing to begin in Greenland.
In a statement posted on his Truth Social platform, Mr. Trump said "Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland," but did not give more details.
The president added that "there are Experts that are saying that the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the World."
Mr. Trump also touted Greenland's role in the defense of the United States in Europe, saying that "any future attack" on the U.S. would have to come across the semi-autonomous island, "where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet conceived."
"It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!" Mr. Trump added.
The announcement comes more than four weeks after the U.S., Greenland and Denmark, which oversees the territory, signed a new security agreement to bolster American military and security presence on the island.
That agreement, which gives the U.S. broad access to the island's airspace and territory, largely focuses on using Greenland for military purposes, but also mentions resource extraction and "minerals cooperation" between the two countries, without specifying any details.
The plan allows the U.S. to expand the existing Pituffik Space Base, the northernmost U.S. military installation which serves as an early-warning system for incoming missiles. The agreement also says the U.S. can establish additional bases at the sites known as Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, which are roughly 950 miles apart. Any of the three parties can propose more "defense areas" as needed, subject to approval by the others.
The deal, which has no expiration date, also blocks non-NATO countries from establishing bases on the island without agreement from the parties.
Since his first term, Mr. Trump had cited Greenland's strategic location as one of the reasons for greater U.S. control over the semi-autonomous island, and even suggested purchasing the island from Denmark or using military force.
Some industry experts believe mineral resources in Greenland have only been lightly explored and up until now the cost of extraction has not made economic sense for private companies.
Kathryn  Watson contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: New knee arthritis treatment delivers lasting pain relief without surgery
articles.title_zh: New knee arthritis treatment delivers lasting pain relief without surgery
articles.content_orig:
A minimally invasive procedure that targets abnormal blood vessels in the knee could provide lasting relief for people struggling with osteoarthritis, offering a potential alternative to joint replacement surgery.
In a study involving 194 patients, researchers found that a treatment using tiny particles that dissolve within hours was associated with substantial reductions in knee pain and improvements in mobility. The benefits persisted for at least 12 months, with 80% of patients assessed at the one-year follow-up reporting clinically meaningful pain relief.
The approach, known as genicular artery embolization, aims to interrupt the inflammation and abnormal blood vessel growth that contribute to chronic knee pain. Rather than replacing the damaged joint, doctors use a thin catheter to deliver microscopic particles directly into specific blood vessels.
The findings, published in the journal Radiology , suggest that this technique could provide another option for patients who have exhausted conventional treatments but cannot or do not want to undergo knee replacement surgery.
Why Knee Arthritis Is So Difficult To Treat
Osteoarthritis is the world's most common form of arthritis and a major cause of disability. According to the World Health Organization, knee osteoarthritis affects more than 365 million adults worldwide.
The condition develops as cartilage, the protective tissue that cushions the ends of bones, gradually deteriorates. But osteoarthritis involves more than cartilage damage. Inflammation within the joint, changes in surrounding tissues, and increased sensitivity of pain signaling nerves can all contribute to persistent discomfort.
For many people, the consequences extend far beyond occasional knee pain. Everyday activities such as walking, climbing stairs, exercising, or standing for extended periods can become increasingly difficult.
Treatments typically begin with physical therapy, medication, and injections into the affected joint. When these approaches stop providing adequate relief, knee replacement surgery may eventually be considered. However, surgery is not appropriate or desirable for everyone.
"For many patients with knee osteoarthritis, there is a real treatment gap today," said Florian Nima Fleckenstein, M.D., deputy head of Interventional Radiology Campus Mitte, Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin. "Conservative measures such as intra-articular injections no longer provide sufficient relief, but joint replacement is not an option for medical or personal reasons."
A Different Way To Fight Knee Arthritis Pain
The treatment being investigated, genicular artery embolization (GAE), approaches knee arthritis from an unusual direction. Instead of focusing directly on damaged cartilage, it targets the abnormal blood vessels that develop around an inflamed joint.
These vessels can form within and around the synovium, a thin membrane lining the inside of the joint. As the vessels multiply, they can contribute to inflammation and encourage the growth of sensory nerves involved in transmitting pain.
GAE is designed to interrupt this process by reducing blood flow through the abnormal vessels while preserving the knee's normal circulation.
During the procedure, an interventional radiologist inserts a thin catheter into an artery and carefully guides it toward the affected blood vessels. Tiny particles are then injected to block selected vessels, with the goal of reducing inflammation and pain.
The technique is called superselective embolization because doctors target specific small arteries rather than blocking circulation throughout the joint. It does not require an open surgical incision or replacement of the knee.
Researchers have previously investigated both temporary blocking agents and permanent microscopic particles. Each approach has potential drawbacks, including differences in how precisely the particles can be delivered and how long they remain inside the blood vessels.
For this study, the team examined rapidly resorbable, gelatin-based microspheres. These precisely sized, spherical particles are engineered to dissolve within hours, potentially combining the advantages of temporary agents with the controlled delivery of permanent microspheres.
"GAE is a whole new treatment regimen that targets abnormal hypervascularity around the joint and, in turn, modulates the pathological neurovascular environment," Dr. Fleckenstein said.
Hypervascularity refers to an unusually high concentration of blood vessels. The pathological neurovascular environment describes the abnormal interactions between those vessels and pain signaling nerves in the affected tissue.
"By reducing both inflammation and pain, GAE with resorbable microspheres may be the first procedure that alters the course of the disease, slowing its progression."
Whether the procedure can actually slow osteoarthritis progression remains an open question. Although reducing inflammation could theoretically influence the disease, the study did not demonstrate that GAE prevents cartilage deterioration or reverses existing joint damage.
Nearly 200 Patients Underwent the Procedure
To evaluate the approach, researchers conducted a prospective single-center study involving 194 patients with osteoarthritis-related knee pain. The participants included 114 women and 80 men, with a median age of 69 years and a median body mass index of 28.4.
All had continued to experience symptoms despite at least three months of conventional care, including physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medications, and injections into the knee.
"We believe these results carry real weight because they come from real-world data," Dr. Fleckenstein said. "With this broad, inclusive study design, our participants are exactly the patients that physicians encounter every day in their practices."
The procedures took place between July and November 2024. Forty-five participants (23%) had osteoarthritis affecting both knees and received two separate treatments, with the second performed within four weeks of the first.
Altogether, the researchers carried out 239 GAE procedures.
Doctors used real-time X-ray imaging, known as fluoroscopy, to guide the catheter and deliver the particles to the targeted arteries. All 239 procedures were technically successful, meaning the intended blood vessels were successfully treated.
The safety findings were also encouraging. No moderate or severe adverse events were recorded, and mild, temporary complications occurred in 6.7% of procedures.
These included brief skin discoloration near the treated area and one superficial collection of blood near the catheter insertion site. All resolved without lasting complications.
Knee Arthritis Pain Dropped and Stayed Lower for a Year
The researchers monitored pain, movement, and quality of life before treatment and at several intervals afterward. Assessments were conducted at six weeks, three months, six months, and 12 months. An orthopedic surgeon also examined patients in person at the six-month follow-up.
Participant retention remained relatively high throughout the study. Follow-up rates were 94% at six weeks (183/194), 89% at three months (172/194), 89% at six months (171/194), and 79% at 12 months (154/194).
The most striking finding was the sustained reduction in knee pain.
Using the Numeric Rating Scale (a 0-to-10 measure of pain intensity), median pain scores fell from 7 before treatment to 4 after six weeks. By six months, the median score had declined to 3, and it remained at that level at the 12-month follow-up.
That represents a reduction of more than half from the original median pain score, with benefits that were still apparent a full year after treatment.
"In our cohort, we saw a significant drop in pain and a significant increase in function, including sports and recreation and daily activity," Dr. Fleckenstein said. "Most importantly, their quality of life significantly increased."

articles.title_orig: U.S. probe of Rep. Ilhan Omar focuses on birth date, citizenship papers, people familiar say
articles.title_zh: U.S. probe of Rep. Ilhan Omar focuses on birth date, citizenship papers, people familiar say
articles.content_orig:
Dem Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar's husband, Tim Mynett, appears at Washington, D.C., home after a raid by HSI agents amid a criminal fraud investigation into the congresswoman's immigration paperwork. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
The husband of Rep. Ilhan Omar , D-Minn., was captured on camera by Fox News Digital entering their shared Washington, D.C., residence the day after it was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents.
Tim Mynett, a political consultant, was walking with a yellow Labrador dog on a leash Tuesday afternoon before entering the home that was searched early Monday morning amid a federal investigation into Omar's immigration status.
His outing came the same day U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro announced her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures about reporting of the couple's shared worth.
Two sources close to HSI’s investigation say the raid was part of a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman's immigration paperwork , which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.
ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME
Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)
Omar’s husband is at the center of one of the congresswoman's most prominent controversies after her financial disclosure filings decreased significantly in reported worth within the span of one filing period.
Pirro revealed her office is now investigating Omar's financial disclosures after the Office of Congressional Conduct in September dropped its misconduct investigation into the congresswoman. Tuesday's announcement opens a new chapter of investigations into the Minnesota Democrat.
The controversy surrounding Omar’s finances began when a 2024 financial report estimated that Omar and Mynett possessed between $6 million and $30 million in assets, all while the Minnesota fraud scandal within the Somali community was beginning to come to fruition.
The largest change in the documents was from Mynett’s assets. His reported ownership interests in both his winery and venture capital advisory firm, which were previously valued in the millions of dollars, are listed with no value now.
In Omar’s 2024 financial disclosure records, Mynett’s share in his winery was valued between $1 million and $5 million, and his share at the venture capital advisory firm was valued between $5 million and $25 million. Now, his equity interests are both listed at $0.
OMAR DUCKS QUESTIONS AS SCRUTINY GROWS OVER FILINGS THAT SLASHED HER REPORTED WEALTH BY MILLIONS
Omar's office previously told Fox News Digital that Mynett has partners in both businesses and said the earlier disclosure mistakenly reflected the businesses' total equity rather than his ownership interest. The office also said the original filing listed assets without accounting for liabilities.
Mynett was a partner of a firm that worked on Omar’s 2020 re-election campaign. The two announced their marriage in March 2020.
This is Omar’s third marriage, but not her most controversial. The "Squad" Democrat has also come under fire for her first marriage to a man many alleged to be her brother. Critics and skeptics claim the two married as part of an immigration scheme .
WATCH: ILHAN OMAR DENIES FEDS HAVE CONTACTED HER AFTER BORDER CZAR HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION
When White House border czar Tom Homan first announced a criminal investigation into Omar, many speculated it would be related to the allegations that she married her brother to evade United States immigration laws. But a former federal prosecutor recently confirmed to Fox News Digital that the statute of limitations would make opening an investigation into the matter difficult.

articles.title_orig: Federal judge issues longer-term decision blocking Trump’s White House media ban
articles.title_zh: Federal judge issues longer-term decision blocking Trump’s White House media ban
articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: What to know about Pope Leo’s diagnosis, leading Democrat rules out 2028 run, and new dinosaur species identified
A federal judge issued an order late Tuesday blocking the Trump administration from banning CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House complex while the organizations’ lawsuit over access proceeds.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly of Washington, D.C., issued the preliminary injunction in the wake of a hearing Thursday at which the administration contended it imposed the ban in part because of national security concerns; media organizations said it was because of “viewpoint discrimination.”
Kelly sided with the news outlets, noting that Trump used national security as a reason for the ban after their press passes had already been revoked and ruling that it also likely violated reporters’ freedom of speech and due process rights.
“There is practically nothing national security-related in the record connected to the President’s decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes to which the Court can defer,” Kelly wrote in his 26-page opinion.
His order will give the outlets access to the White House until the underlying lawsuit challenging the ban is resolved. But it doesn’t require the administration to allow reporters from the outlets access to the Oval Office or Air Force One — locations where the administration has blocked reporters from CNN and Politico in recent weeks.
Trump vowed to appeal on Truth Social before the ruling was handed down. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment following the ruling.
Kelly had issued a temporary restraining order lifting the ban while he weighed whether to issue an injunction.
Trump announced the bans of CNN, MS NOW and Politico on social media on Sept. 18, saying they were a “result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he wrote on Truth Social.
In court filings, the three news organizations said the ban affected 78 journalists who had “hard passes,” meaning they had been previously screened and credentialed to work at the White House.
The outlets filed a lawsuit alleging Trump’s action violated their due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the suit said.
The White House and Trump then began arguing that the ban was intended to address national security concerns, with Trump saying in another post that the outlets’ reporting was “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”
The judge was unmoved by that argument.
Kelly said it was clear from Trump’s announcement of the ban and from subsequent remarks that his motivation was content.
“President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him,” Kelly wrote, finding this decision violated the journalists’ First and Fifth amendment rights.
He noted, however, that his decision doesn’t concede that Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness are unfounded or that the government is “powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”
Kelly cited Trump’s recent remarks to Time magazine that he didn’t like “bad story after bad story” coming from CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists. It was, Ted Boutrous, the news outlets’ attorney, had argued ahead of the decision, “a confession of what amounts to viewpoint discrimination.”
“President Trump, I’ll give him credit,” Boutrous said. “He’s not hiding it.”
In his previous decision, Kelly also found that the administration had denied the outlets due process under settled law from several cases that have made their way to the D.C. federal appeals court.
The White House argued that the appeals court decisions were wrong.
“Maybe—but this Court is bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop,” Kelly wrote.
At a hearing on the injunction Thursday, the Justice Department lawyer representing the White House, Michael Velchik, asked Kelly to lift his restraining order, calling the White House a “sacred place” that shouldn’t have to give people access just because they “identify as a reporter.”
“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” Velchik said.
Boutrous argued that the administration was engaging in impermissible and unconstitutional “viewpoint discrimination” because the ban was based on Trump’s dislike of the outlets’ reporting and because he has said he hoped the ban would force journalists to “straighten themselves out.”
In court filings, Boutrous urged Kelly to ignore the national security arguments, saying they were manufactured and not what the case is really about.
Boutrous argued that “the President himself has continued telling anyone who will listen precisely what this ban is really about, most recently complaining at length in an interview with Time magazine that he banned Plaintiffs because he feels that he should not ‘be forced to bear’ what he considers ‘constantly bad stories,’ as he ‘won the election’ and has ‘done great things.’”
After Tuesday night’s ruling, Boutrous said he and his clients were grateful to the court for securing their access anew.
“The President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like,” he said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban.’”
Separately, the Justice Department said last week that it was investigating five major TV networks , including CNN and NBC, for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of Trump as a result of the ban against the three news outlets.
The pool is a rotating group of networks that share the duties of recording a president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The on-duty network then distributes information and media, such as video and audio, to other outlets for their use.
Dareh Gregorian is a politics reporter for NBC News.
Gary Grumbach is an NBC News legal affairs reporter, based in Washington, D.C.

articles.title_orig: Skipping Secularism: 2 Clues from the End of the World
articles.title_zh: Skipping Secularism: 2 Clues from the End of the World
articles.content_orig:
The world is a confusing place right now. We believe that faithful proclamation of the gospel is what our hostile and disoriented world needs. Do you believe that too? Help TGC bring biblical wisdom to the confusing issues across the world by making a gift to our international work.
Maybe it was the whale meat I was eating. Or the earlier round of herring shark. But as I asked questions of my new friends on the Faroe Islands, my view of secularism began to fill up and fill in. They gave me two new clues in my efforts to understand and ultimately reverse the conditions of Western secularism.
When you visit the Faroe Islands, you can’t take your eyes off the scenery—especially on rare days when the sun shines.
As I wrote about after my visit to Copenhagen last year , we can see the conditions that have delivered storm clouds of secularism across much of northern Europe. The combination of Protestantism and established churches has dismantled Christian belief and especially practice in the region.
In this land, the light of gospel radiates more brightly than anywhere else in the Nordic region
The exception can be found on the Faroe Islands, whose windswept fjords feel like the end of world, amid the vast Atlantic Ocean between Iceland and Norway, north of the Shetland and Hebrides isles. In this land where the sun almost never shines (no city in the whole world is gloomier than the Faroese capital, Tórshavn) the light of gospel radiates more brightly than anywhere else in the Nordic region.
Why? I asked my gracious hosts as they fed me from the bounty of the sea, as they drove me through horizontal rains around mountain turns, as they honored their ancestors with the story of their persevering faith.
The first clue came in our visit to Fuglafjørður, situated in the northeast on the island of Eysturoy. From our host we learned about his great-grandfather, the 20th-century Brethren missionary and Bible translator Victor Danielsen.
The statue outside his former church commemorates Danielsen’s most notable accomplishment, the first Bible translated for the common people in Faroese instead of the colonial Danish. Today, the Brethren compose at least 10 percent of the islands’ population of some 55,000, including the 29-year-old prime minister, who was on my flight to Copenhagen. He planned to meet with the Danish king.
The Faroese treasure their independence within the Danish Commonwealth. Not until 1938 did the Faroe Islands secure Danish permission to use Faroese in their churches and schools. It’s no coincidence that Danielsen’s New Testament translation published one year earlier, in 1937 .
Early Brethren missionaries from the United Kingdom saw no spiritual fruit from their labors for two decades. But with Danielsen’s ministry, the Brethren became champions of the ordinary Faroese, who trace ethnic roots to the British Isles, shared colonial identity to Greenland, and remote island affinity to Iceland.
I’ve observed in studies of secularism in the modern West that thriving Christian movements require medium tension with their host cultures. But opposition isn’t sufficient. The Brethren wouldn’t have gained a missionary foothold only by criticizing Lutheran state religion. Resisting secularism requires channeling the aspirations of the people too.
The Brethren set themselves apart with a high view of biblical authority and countercultural holiness, traits that still characterize their followers even as they’ve ascended into the islands’ globally engaged business elite. But they also came to embody native Faroese values and aspirations as a free and independent people, proud of their ancient island culture. In this they resemble the history of Presbyterian missions in Korea as well as the Persian culture that at least last decade held out against Islamic hegemony in Iran.
After preaching Esther 4 in view of the lovely fjord village of Norðragøta, I spoke with Brethren who have earned PhDs in the United Kingdom, opposed abortion and gay marriage in the Faroese Parliament, and traveled the world to represent local business interests (at least 90 percent of the islands’ exports relate to the fishing industry).
For such a remote setting, the high standard of living surprised me. The Faroes’ GDP per capita exceeds Denmark , even if it falls short of the world-leading Norwegians and their vast oil reserves. Many of the homes appeared new, compared to what I’ve seen in other Nordic countries. Over that succulent meal of whale and shark, I learned that the prosperity dates back only about 30 years, and especially in the last 15, due to the success of salmon farming and rising fish prices, following a collapse of the Faroe economy in the 1990s.
Once again, Faroese Christianity bucks the trend, providing the second clue. Economic development is supposed to deliver secularism. That’s the story Denmark and other Nordic countries tell of their “modern breakthrough,” the transition from the backward, rural 19th century to the progressive, urbane 20th.
But what if secularism is less of an economic inevitability and more of a philosophical fad taking root in the developed West roughly between the 1860s and 1960s? And what if lack of economic development during that century shielded some cultures from the full effects of secularism? Even when those cultures catch up, they don’t necessarily descend the whole ladder to secularism.
In this regard, the Faroe Islands could be similar to regions of the United States, especially the Southeast, that developed later and thus far retain much higher rates of Christian belief and observance compared to regions that prospered during that earlier period. And like the Southeast, the Faroe Islands have become a missionary engine, launching gospel workers throughout Europe and even around the world.
Have my new friends in the Faroe Islands helped cracked the code to Christian endurance amid secularism? I wouldn’t put anything past these resilient people tucked inside treeless mountains on the shores of the mighty Atlantic.
What if secularism is less of an economic inevitability and more of a philosophical fad?
Perhaps the period of acute secularism could be skipped, and we’re not waiting for another shoe to drop as the Faroe Islands prosper. Perhaps the Brethren have charted a course for us from the edge of the world. Moderate cultural opposition is necessary but not sufficient. The gospel’s indigenizing principle must also capture the aspirations of people made in the image of God as they enjoy his common grace.
Big breakthroughs can start in small places. Of all people, Christians know that story.
The Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics helps Christians share the truth,
    goodness, and beauty of the gospel as the only hope that fulfills our deepest
    longings. We want to train Christians—everyone from pastors to parents to
    professors—to boldly share the good news of Jesus Christ in a way that clearly
    communicates to this secular age.
Click the button below to sign up for updates and announcements from The Keller Center.
Collin Hansen serves as vice president for content and editor in chief of The Gospel Coalition, as well as executive director of The Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics . He hosts the Gospelbound podcast, writes the weekly Unseen Things newsletter, and has written and contributed to many books, including Timothy Keller: His Spiritual and Intellectual Formation and Rediscover Church: Why the Body of Christ Is Essential . He has published with the New York Times and the Washington Post and offered commentary for CNN, Fox News, NPR, BBC, ABC News, and PBS NewsHour . He edited The Gospel After Christendom , The AI Apocalypse , and The New City Catechism Devotional , among other books. He is an adjunct professor at Beeson Divinity School , where he has co-chaired the advisory board.

articles.title_orig: Mike Collins Attacks Back: 7 Takeaways From the Second Senate Debate in Georgia
articles.title_zh: Mike Collins Attacks Back: 7 Takeaways From the Second Senate Debate in Georgia
articles.content_orig:
One Republican tried to put distance between herself and President Donald Trump on trade and the Iran war. Another focused her criticism on Trump’s diesel deal with Russia. And a third tried to turn one of the GOP’s biggest political liabilities against their Democratic rival.
Tuesday’s Senate debates in Maine, Georgia and Iowa offered a revealing look at how Republicans are navigating a difficult political environment in the closing weeks before the midterm elections, with control of the narrowly divided Senate at stake.
In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins emphasized her independence from Trump as she sparred with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson over the Iran war, healthcare cuts and a trade war with Canada. Down the East Coast in Georgia, Republican Rep. Mike Collins went on the offensive as he tried to turn the tables by attacking Sen. Jon Ossoff over his ties to a donor named in the Jeffrey Epstein files — an issue that has largely put Republicans on the defensive.
In another closely watched contest in Iowa, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek made their case to voters Tuesday night for the state’s open Senate contest, squabbling over Trump’s foreign policy and which of the two candidates actually showed up for work.
The heated exchanges underscore the different challenges facing Republicans as they try to hold onto their Senate majority. Democrats, meanwhile, need a net gain of four seats to flip the Senate.
Here’s a look at key moments from the debates.
In Maine, Susan Collins sought to emphasize her independence, as the five-term incumbent seeks reelection in an environment increasingly difficult for Republicans amidst the president’s plummeting popularity.
After kicking off with her criticism of his approach to the war in Iran, Collins during later exchanges pointed to her vote against Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and her opposition to the tariffs on Canada. Her debate performance was the latest example of how vulnerable Republicans are defying Trump ahead of the midterms.
When discussing the Iran war, Collins quickly called Trump out for not having a plan, and stressed how once the conflict surpassed 60 days, she voted against the war effort.
“I voted with the Democrats to bring the war to an end, but there were not sufficient votes for that to happen,” the senator said. “In addition, I agree that the president did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which part of the world’s oil travels, and I don’t feel that that was well anticipated, although it should have been.”
While Jackson sought to tie Collins to her party’s signature tax and policy bill that cut Medicaid, Collins pointed out that she ultimately did not support the bill specifically because of those cuts.
When Collins was asked about her position on Trump’s tariffs on Canada , she said, “I have been extremely outspoken in my opposition to Canadian tariffs and I have voted repeatedly to repeal them.”
But while Collins sought to highlight her distance from Trump, she also argued that she was better equipped than Jackson to work with his administration, pointing to her position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee as leverage in negotiations.
Hinson similarly sought to distance herself from Trump during her Iowa debate on two of the biggest foreign policy crises confronting the president — Russia’s war with Ukraine and the US war with Iran.
On Tuesday night she criticized Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply markets with diesel fuel in a bid to lower prices that both candidates said are hurting Iowa farmers.
“We need to lower diesel prices, but I don’t think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it,” she said.
Hinson also pointed to a 2022 congressional ban on energy imports from Russia, a measure intended to punish the Russian economy over Putin’s decision to invade Ukraine.
“I am proud to have voted for sanctions against Russia,” she said. “I’m banned from Russia because of my stance on being tough on them and supporting Ukraine, and we cannot allow Vladimir Putin to win that war.”
She also said Trump’s war with Iran “does need to come to a resolute and successful end as quickly as possible.” However, Hinson balked when asked whether she would again vote against a war powers resolution that would halt Trump’s ability to continue military action against Iran without the approval of Congress.
“I don’t think we need another resolution on the House floor. I think the president and the US military can bring it to the end,” she said.
Those breaks with Trump were notable in a debate in which Trump played a minor role — a reality owing to both Hinson’s awareness of Trump’s sagging popularity and Turek’s need to win over a share of voters who backed Trump in the 2024 election.
Hinson rarely made direct reference to Trump. But she did say she lobbied Trump personally last week to quickly get soybean trade pacts negotiated to open up foreign markets for Midwestern farmers — an acknowledgement of the economic fallout of Trump’s tariff policies.
Mike Collins spent the first Georgia Senate debate largely on the defensive. But in Tuesday’s debate, he came out swinging.
“This is a race between Georgia and Georgetown,” Collins said at the top of his opening state.
From there, Collins called Ossoff a “globetrotting trust-fund kid,” and a “coward” who hides behind “scripted online clips.” And days after Ossoff opened their last debate by telling Georgians he would put Collins’ record on trial, the Republican said it was his turn to expose his opponent’s past.
“Tough questions are going to come out tonight,” Collins said. “No one’s ever challenged Jon Ossoff on anything he’s ever voted on.”
Collins, who faces an uphill climb to knock off the incumbent Democrat, spent much of the next hour criticizing Ossoff over his record on immigration, his support for green energy initiatives and the help he’s received from LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman. He accused Ossoff of being an inadequate ally of Israel and of ignoring the interests of Georgians while he built a national profile that has fueled speculation about a future White House bid.
“He’s using us as a platform,” Collins said in his closing remarks. “Georgians are hardworking people, and we deserve a senator that will work as hard as us for us.”
For his part, Ossoff picked up where he left off at last week’s debate. He confronted Collins over his White nationalist son-in-law , criticized his support for Trump’s tariffs and tied him to the unpopular conflict with Iran. He also repeatedly pressed Collins to testify in a House ethics investigation into whether his office misused taxpayer funds.
Collins called the investigation a “political hit job” when asked. Ossoff contended he was dodging.
A testy back-and-forth in the Georgia Senate debate over files related to Jeffrey Epstein illustrated how the late financier’s crimes continue to roil American politics.
During the debate, Mike Collins attacked Ossoff over the donations he’s received from Hoffman — “the same guy that’s in the Epstein files.”
(After the Justice Department’s Epstein files showed several messages between Hoffman and Epstein, the prolific Democratic donor acknowledged he had multiple meetings with the disgraced financier. “I only knew Jeffrey Epstein because of a fundraising relationship with MIT, which I very much regret,” Hoffman wrote on X .)
“The Epstein class is on stage right now, and it’s you,” Collins said, pressing Ossoff to denounce Hoffman.
Ossoff shot back that Collins was against making the Epstein files public, a reference to a July 2025 House vote that blocked a measure that would have required the Department of Justice to release the records in 30 days. articles.title_zh: Trump Adds Another Giveaway to His Midterm Pitch: Pardons.
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump provided clemency to mechanics charged under the Biden-era Department of Justice for conspiracy to violate the Clean Air Act onstage Tuesday at a rally in Alaska.
President Donald Trump announced pardons for two Alaska diesel mechanics during a midterm rally Tuesday night in Wasilla, bringing the men onstage to sign clemency documents as he highlighted major energy investments and infrastructure projects in the Last Frontier.
Trump identified Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming, two co-owners of an Anchorage diesel repair shop who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to violate the Clean Air Act in 2022.
"I'm giving each one of the three an unconditional pardon," Trump told supporters, also referring to an earlier pardon for Mackenzie "Mac" Spurlock, a Wasilla diesel shop owner.
TRUMP GRANTS PARDONS TO 'PERSECUTED' MECHANICS IN RIGHT-TO-REPAIR CRACKDOWN: 'I AM SETTING THEM ALL FREE'
President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a campaign rally at Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center on Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska. (AFP via Getty Images)
The president defended the men, saying their work helped keep trucks operating in Alaska's extreme cold and arguing that their Biden-era prosecutions were unfair.
According to the Biden Justice Department , Czubak and Fleming were among three co-owners of "Arm Rippin Toys" who admitted removing federally required emissions-control equipment and tampering with monitoring devices on at least 37 diesel vehicles between July 2019 and September 2020.
BIDEN-ERA ENVIRO RULE ACCUSED OF STRANGLING TRUCKERS, SQUEEZING AMERICANS LANDS ON TRUMP CHOPPING BLOCK
Supporters listen as President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally at Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center on Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska. (AFP via Getty Images)
The shop collected approximately $100,000 for the modifications, federal prosecutors said at the time.
As he signed the clemency documents, Trump took a jab at former President Joe Biden's use of an autopen .
"So I'm going to sign this now, something that Joe Biden would be unable to do because he was unable to sign his signature," Trump said.
TRUMP COMMUTES SENTENCE FOR FORMER PHILADELPHIA UNION OFFICIAL, ATTORNEY SAYS
President Donald Trump greets supporters as he arrives to speak during a campaign rally ahead of next month's midterms at Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center on Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska. (AFP via Getty Images)
He also shared candidly the privilege of the presidential pardon power with the crowd.
"What an honor. I love doing this stuff," Trump said.
One of the men thanked the president from the stage, describing the personal impact of the prosecution.
"It really did destroy us. It destroyed friendships. It destroyed families," he said.

The pardons came during a rally in which Trump made a series of major announcements about Alaska's energy future , including declaring that a long-awaited 800-mile natural gas pipeline had secured every necessary federal permit.
"Every single permit that you need, you can start tonight," Trump told the crowd. "Every single permit that you need has been granted."
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for additional details on the project's federal permitting status.

articles.title_orig: China's export engine hits fastest pace since February with 36% growth
articles.title_zh: China's export engine hits fastest pace since February with 36% growth
articles.content_orig:
China's producer price index climbed at its fastest pace in over four years, rising 5% in September as higher fuel prices pushed up costs for businesses.
The increase was higher than the 4.5% expected by economists polled by Reuters, and sharply up from  the 3.8% seen in the previous month.
China's National Bureau of Statistics said higher prices were also seen in the country's coal sector, due to increased demand for coal for winter heating, temporary tight supply in major coal-producing areas, and expectations of rising international coal prices.
Consumer prices saw a 0.9% rise, marginally missing expectations of 1%, but up from 0.8% in the month before.
The increase in the consumer inflation rate was due to gasoline prices, which climbed 16.6% and contributed approximately 0.47 percentage points to the year-on-year CPI increase, according to Dong Lijuan, chief statistician of the Urban Division at the NBS.
This was partially offset by a wider fall in food prices, which declined 1.7% and pulled down the CPI by 0.29 percentage points, Dong added.
The core CPI rate, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, climbed 1%.
The lower-than-expected CPI reading indicates that domestic demand remains "lackluster," according to Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, in a note after the data release.
However, the higher PPI is pointing to an economy that is gradually moving away from deflationary pressures even if the recovery remains uneven, said Hao Zhou, chief economist at Guotai Junan International Holdings.
His view was that domestic demand was recovering more gradually than the industrial sector, although the fact that consumer inflation has remained in positive territory indicated at the deflationary environment in 2024 and 2025 "is continuing to fade."
The higher inflation figures come as China's economy grapples with its lowest growth rate in more than three years . GDP growth for the second quarter of the year missed expectations at 4.3%.
While economic data for August showed that retail sales expanded more slowly than expected, industrial output beat expectations.
On Sept 28, a State Council readout signaled that more policy support could be on the way for the Chinese economy, saying that "In response to emerging challenges in the economy's operation, efforts should be made to intensify counter-cyclical adjustment of macro policies."
Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, wrote that "It marks a bit of a shift in tone," adding that more policy support rollouts will be coming so as to reach both short- and long-term growth targets.
"These include the 4.5%-5.0% GDP growth target for 2026, and the longstanding goal to double GDP from 2020 to 2035."

articles.title_orig: Launch of 13 new African National Youth Chapters of the World Food Forum
articles.title_zh: Launch of 13 new African National Youth Chapters of the World Food Forum
articles.content_orig:
Thirteen new World Food Forum (WFF) National Youth Chapters in Africa have joined the growing network of young leaders working to transform agrifood systems across the continent. They are in: Benin, Botswana, Burundi, Comoros, Democratic Republic of Congo, Eswatini, Gabon, Lesotho, Namibia, Nigeria, São Tomé and Príncipe, Senegal and Togo.
These new chapters bring the total number of National Youth Chapters in Africa to 33.
Speaking at the launch during the Global Youth Forum of the World Food Forum, FAO Assistant Director-General and Regional Representative for Africa Abebe Haile-Gabriel emphasized the importance of sustained investment in youth leadership.
“The real measure of success will be our ability to sustain this momentum, scale investment, and ensure that young people are not just beneficiaries of change, but architects of Africa's agrifood systems transformation,” he said.
Creating opportunities for youth leadership
The National Youth Chapters provide platforms for young people to connect, share knowledge, build partnerships and contribute to agrifood systems transformation at national and regional levels.
With more than 60 percent of Africa's population under the age of 25, expanding opportunities for young people to participate in decision-making, innovation and entrepreneurship is critical to the continent's future.
FAO is strengthening youth engagement across Africa through capacity-building initiatives, partnerships and opportunities for young agripreneurs to contribute to policy discussions.
Young agribusiness entrepreneurs and advocates from across Africa are participating at the World Food Forum in Rome this week. Youth leadership will also feature prominently at the upcoming Africa Science & Innovation Forum taking place in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, from 27 to 29 October.
Empowering Africa’s youth was also the focus of a session at the World Food Forum today titled Leading from the Front: Africa’s Youth Driving Agrifood Systems Transformation, featuring FAO’s Abebe Haile-Gabriel and Lesotho’s Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and Nutrition, Selibe Mochoboroane. The session focused on expanding opportunities for young Africans to lead innovation, entrepreneurship and job creation across agrifood systems. Haile-Gabriel emphasized the importance of investing in young people's skills, improving access to finance and technology, and ensuring young people have a meaningful role in shaping policies and investments.
The 13 new chapters join existing chapters in Cabo Verde, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia, the Gambia, Ghana, Kenya, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mauritius, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Africa, South Sudan, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine received no intel about incoming missiles, Zelenskyy says
articles.title_zh: Ukraine received no intel about incoming missiles, Zelenskyy says
articles.content_orig:
A Russian ballistic missile hit a power plant in Kyiv on Tuesday evening, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, without Ukraine receiving advance warning from its Western allies and despite US President Donald Trump's claim for an "energy ceasefire" in effect.
Ukraine depends heavily on Western intelligence, especially from the US, to detect incoming Russian attacks and identify its own targets.
Kyiv, home to about three million people, has faced intensifying attacks from Russian drones and missiles, with energy infrastructure a key target.
"A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote on Facebook.
"The main target was energy infrastructure, specifically the CHP-4. Unfortunately, it was hit."
AFP journalists also reported hearing several blasts in the Ukrainian capital.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine's systems detected the missiles only as they neared the city.
"This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added.
At least two people were killed in the same attack, which also struck a residential building in the Desnianskyi district, said Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko. Around 20 others were wounded, he said.
Overnight from Monday into Tuesday, Kyiv residents heard explosions from Russian strikes before the air raid sirens sounded, something that has happened only rarely in the past.
On Tuesday, Ukrainian officials said the situation was due to the Russian military's use of hard-to-detect missiles or possible technical issues.
US President Trump caused confusion on Sunday with a surprise "energy ceasefire" announcement on his Truth Social network, saying Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop their punishing long-range strikes on power plants and oil refineries.
Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy over strikes on Russian oil refineries and on Saturday suggested it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".

articles.title_orig: Rare Nanotyrannus skeleton goes on display at NYC Sotheby's before heading to historic auction
articles.title_zh: Rare Nanotyrannus skeleton goes on display at NYC Sotheby's before heading to historic auction
articles.content_orig:
On quick glance, the fossil unveiled Tuesday at a Manhattan auction house looks like an undersized Tyrannosaurus rex , with its signature gaping jaw filled with razor sharp teeth. But the proportions are off, as its arms and legs are much too long.
That’s because the dinosaur skeleton isn’t actually a T. rex but a recently confirmed distant cousin. The Nanotyrannus, as this smaller, nimbler predator is known, is on view in the lobby of Sotheby’s headquarters ahead of its Oct. 27 auction.
Standing 6.5 feet (2 meters) tall and stretching nearly 20 feet (6 meters) long, the rare fossil is one of only three such skeletons known to exist.
“What’s really exciting is that until they proved this genus existed, we thought that T. rex was the only apex predator of the Cretaceous,” said Cassandra Hatton, a vice chair at Sotheby’s. “We now know that they coexisted. They lived alongside each other, occupying distinct niches in the ecological system.”
A decades-long scientific debate kicked off with the 1942 discovery of what’s now considered the first Nanotyrannus head, the so-called “Cleveland Skull” housed at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History.
Fast forward to October 2025, when new research concluded that the Nanotyrannus was in fact a distinct genus of dinosaur that coexisted with T. rex.
Scientists examining the growth rings within preserved bones found the dinosaurs were fully formed adults, not juveniles. The research challenged long-held assumptions that the mighty “King of the Tyrant Lizards” was the sole large predator of the Cretaceous period, some 67 million years ago.
“It’s like a lion and a cheetah,” Hatton explains. “They hunted different prey. They were around at the same time. It’s possible T. rex ate these.”
Indeed, there are more than 150 key differences between the Nanotyrannus and T. rex, the most noticeable being their sizes.
At about 18 feet (5.5 meters) long, an adult Nanotyrannus was about half the length of an adult T. rex. Instead of the T. rex’s famously stubby arms, its forelimbs were longer and its hand claws were larger.
Nanotyrannus also boasted more and different-looking teeth. Whereas the T. rex’s were bond-crushingly thick and almost banana-shaped, the Nanotyrannus’ were more slender and almost bladelike.
“Those teeth would slash the meat off of the animal it was hunting. It went after faster prey,” Hatton explained of the Nanotyrannus. “You look at a T. rex, it’s big, lumbering. It went after slower prey, and it would eat the whole thing.”
Sotheby’s bills “Jodi,” as the dinosaur fossil is nicknamed, as the “finest and most complete” Nanotyrannus skeleton currently available. Hatton said it’s almost 70% complete, with a virtually complete skull and a jaw that has roughly 35 teeth.
The fossil is named after Jodi Pierson, the Montana rancher who discovered it on her land in 2019. Its discovery and excavation were the focus of the Discovery Channel documentary series “Dino Hunters” in 2020.
“Jodi” was found some 8 miles (13 kilometers) from where the so-called Dueling Dinosaurs fossil — which depicts a Nanotyrannus and a Triceratops — was unearthed in 2006.
That famous specimen, nicknamed “Bloody Mary,” is considered nearly 100% complete, but it’s housed at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences and is not for sale. The third Nanotyrannus skeleton is located at the Burpee Museum of Natural History in Rockford, Illinois.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
The Society of Vertebrate Paleontology, an advocacy group of scientists, scholars and students, has called for significant fossils like “Jodi” to be publicly displayed in museums and other research institutions rather than sold privately.
But Hatton argued that if it wasn’t for the professional dinosaur hunters, the world might not have known that Nanotyrannus existed.
“These people are crucial in the preservation of science,” she said. “We don’t have enough universities and museums out there digging and doing field programs. We absolutely need private diggers who invest their own money to go do this.”
Stuart Sumida, the society’s president and a biology professor at California State University San Bernardino, rejected the notion as a “blatant lie.” The latest auction comes after Sotheby’s sold a T. rex fossil for a record $50.1 million this summer.
“No peer-reviewed scientific study can be published on specimens that are not held in the public trust,” he said. “Once in private hands it can never be studied, and generations of children and adults alike will never see it again.

articles.title_orig: Flu season is arriving months early. Here's where it's spreading
articles.title_zh: Flu season is arriving months early. Here's where it's spreading
articles.content_orig:
by BARBARA MORSE, NBC 10 NEWS
(WJAR)  — We're already seeing an uptick in our fall and winter seasonal illnesses -- especially the flu.
And there are different strains which is why all flu vaccines this year are what's known as trivalent--protecting against three different flu strains.
So who's at highest risk for complications?
"Those 65 and older, those with chronic medical conditions like diabetes, chronic heart disease, kidney disease, liver disease, other lung conditions, those who have asthma, and COPD are most at risk and also small children," said Dr. Charelle Allen,  a family primary care physician for Brown University Health in Taunton.
She said when it comes to flu vaccines, it's not one size fits all.
Doctors are recommending vaccinations as seasonal viruses make an early appearance. (WJAR)
Among them--there are higher doses for those 65 and older, nasal sprays with a weakened live virus for healthy, non pregnant individuals between 2 and 49. Check with your doctor.
"For flu, it's more so of an abrupt onset so you'll have a high fever, you'll feel joint pains, muscle aches, feel really ill," said Allen.
COVID-19 may have similar symptoms.  A test can help sort that out.
Then there's respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV. Its symptoms are somewhat similar.
"For RSV we're looking for like the lower respiratory tract symptoms, such as wheezing, sputum production and cough with mucous," said Allen.
Those 75 and older should be vaccinated, and those 50 to 74 with chronic conditions.
"And then pregnant women, typically offered between 32 and 36 weeks of gestation," said Allen.
Or, it's recommended that babies born between October and March to unvaccinated moms should get the shot within the first week of life.
Bottom line: "Any of these things can lead to bronchitis or pneumonia, so if you are at increased risk, immunocompromised, it's definitely recommended that you get vaccinated," said Allen.

articles.title_orig: In heated Georgia Senate debate, Jon Ossoff says he won’t run for president in 2028
articles.title_zh: In heated Georgia Senate debate, Jon Ossoff says he won’t run for president in 2028
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said Tuesday night during a debate that he will not run for president in 2028.
Ossoff made the statement in response to a question as he faced off with his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff is seeking a second six-year term in Georgia and said he would serve the full term.
“I have zero interest in running for president,” Ossoff said when he was asked directly by one of the moderators. “I’m not running for president. I’m running for re-election to the Senate.”
Ossoff has been regularly discussed as a potential Democratic contender in 2028. If he were to win the presidency, he would have to give up his Senate seat, which he stressed Tuesday night that he would not do.
After the brief remark, Ossoff quickly transitioned to pressing Collins about why he has supported President Donald Trump’s tariffs, a main focus of both his campaign and a debate the two held last week . Tuesday was the second debate in the nationally watched Georgia Senate race, this one organized by the Atlanta Press Club.
Collins quipped that Ossoff was actually trying to run for president and will be “your DSA candidate,” a reference to the Democratic Socialists of America.
The exchange came at the beginning of the hourlong debate, which covered ground including data centers; the economy under Trump, whose approval rating is at record lows; the war in Iran; and the issue of Collins’ son-in-law’s promoting white nationalist posts on social media.
Ossoff asked Collins directly whether he considered himself a “white nationalist.”
“I condemn any sort of hate speech,” Collins said. “Antisemitism, hate of any kind. It’s abhorrent.”
The exchange continued when Collins again asked Ossoff to denounce Reid Hoffman, a major donor to Democratic causes — including Ossoff-aligned political committees — whose name appeared in the Epstein files . Collins brought up Hoffman several times last week and did so again during the second debate.
Ossoff did not directly respond, and he again pointed to the fact that those close to Collins amplified white nationalists’ posts.
“How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for Senate?” Ossoff said. “The paper reported it’s still going on today.”
Given a chance to respond, Collins did not address it directly. But he said rhetoric like Ossoff’s had motivated a New York man who is accused of making death threats against him.
“I’m a little tired of this, Jon,” Collins said. “This crazy person is in jail right now because of your rhetoric.”
Neither candidate directly answered the other’s charges.
Collins also, once again, did not answer questions about whether or not Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. He was asked about audio of a call Trump made after the 2020 election asking Georgia Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “ find 11,780 votes ” to help overturn the 2020 election.
“You know, Joe Biden went into office, and boy, Georgians paid for it,” Collins said.
Matt Dixon is a senior national politics reporter for NBC News, based in Florida.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Energy Giant Struck as War Spikes Between Houthis and Saudi Arabia
articles.title_zh: Saudi Energy Giant Struck as War Spikes Between Houthis and Saudi Arabia
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis traded fresh strikes on energy infrastructure, with the Iran-backed group again targeting the Saudi capital and appearing to hit the headquarters of Saudi state oil giant Aramco.
An administrative building belonging to Aramco in the Eastern Province city of Dhahran, where the company is headquartered, was targeted, according to Saudi authorities. It caused a limited fire, but it’s not clear if this was due to a direct hit or to falling debris. No injuries were reported.
The Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted and destroyed three cruise missiles and two drones targeting the Riyadh region and southern Saudi Arabia. At least four people were injured from falling debris, according to Saudi authorities.
CNN has reached out to Aramco for comment.
It marked the latest escalation between the two sides, following a week of deadly Houthi missile and drone attacks that shut Riyadh’s main international airport .
The strikes also came just hours after Saudi Arabia attacked a key fuel depot on Tuesday, which it claims was being used by Houthi rebels to support strikes on the kingdom’s airports and energy facilities – as well as attacks on shipping in the Red Sea.
Earlier, the Houthi-controlled Yemen Oil Company had said that the facility held no stocks of petroleum products, and that an attack would not affect fuel reserves or supplies.
The strikes killed two civilians and injured two, according to the Houthis, though the Saudi-led coalition insisted it had warned civilians to leave the area beforehand.
“This operation focused on neutralizing the capabilities the Houthi militia uses to threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and maritime corridors,” coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said in a statement.
Tuesday’s exchange comes amid signs the long-running conflict, which reignited this summer and intensified last month after years of relative calm, is continuing to escalate.
Earlier Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched toward its eastern province, and another aimed at Haradh near the Yemeni border. It also reported intercepting three Houthi drones north of Riyadh.
Meanwhile, Houthi-run Al Masirah TV reported that artillery fire by the Saudi-led coalition in Saada province wounded three Yemenis and two African residents in Baqim district. It later reported that two civilians were killed and two others wounded by artillery fire on residential villages in the border district of Shada in Sadaa, and also reported strikes in Sanaa and several other provinces. CNN cannot independently verify the reports.
The conflict has been intensifying since the Houthis announced in July that — in response to what they say is retaliation for a Saudi blockade on the Yemeni capital — they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea as well as infrastructure inside the kingdom.
Those attacks have stepped up in recent days, including with repeated strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, where 13 people were killed and more than 300 wounded on Saturday in what was the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Why billions spent on defense haven’t shielded Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
The US, UK, Spain and Canada are among countries now warning their citizens against using the airport. Meanwhile, the US State Department on Tuesday expanded travel restrictions for US government personnel in the kingdom, saying employees now require special authorization from the chief of mission to use any airport in Saudi Arabia.
The attacks have also exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s defense capabilities as it wages its air campaign in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is fighting the Houthis on the ground.
On Tuesday, the Yemeni government forces claimed to have made continued advances in the military operation, dubbed “Dawn of Yemen.” It said that in the past 24 hours its forces had carried out 2,200 strikes against Houthi positions, killing about 1,200 fighters and destroying or disabling more than 440 military vehicles and other assets. CNN could not independently verify the figures.
Meanwhile, the Houthis vowed further attacks against economic and aviation targets within Saudi Arabia, warning that they would target facilities belonging to Aramco as well as the King Khalid International Airport if Saudi forces continued attacking them.
CNN’s Eyad Kourdi contributed to the report.

articles.title_orig: Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX
articles.title_zh: Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX
articles.content_orig:
Microbiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allege
A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China . With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.
Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only.
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.

articles.title_orig: Ossoff commits to 6-year Senate term amid 2028 speculation
articles.title_zh: Ossoff commits to 6-year Senate term amid 2028 speculation
articles.content_orig:
One Republican tried to put distance between herself and President Donald Trump on trade and the Iran war. Another focused her criticism on Trump’s diesel deal with Russia. And a third tried to turn one of the GOP’s biggest political liabilities against their Democratic rival.
Tuesday’s Senate debates in Maine, Georgia and Iowa offered a revealing look at how Republicans are navigating a difficult political environment in the closing weeks before the midterm elections, with control of the narrowly divided Senate at stake.
In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins emphasized her independence from Trump as she sparred with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson over the Iran war, healthcare cuts and a trade war with Canada. Down the East Coast in Georgia, Republican Rep. Mike Collins went on the offensive as he tried to turn the tables by attacking Sen. Jon Ossoff over his ties to a donor named in the Jeffrey Epstein files — an issue that has largely put Republicans on the defensive.
In another closely watched contest in Iowa, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek made their case to voters Tuesday night for the state’s open Senate contest, squabbling over Trump’s foreign policy and which of the two candidates actually showed up for work.
The heated exchanges underscore the different challenges facing Republicans as they try to hold onto their Senate majority. Democrats, meanwhile, need a net gain of four seats to flip the Senate.
Here’s a look at key moments from the debates.
In Maine, Susan Collins sought to emphasize her independence, as the five-term incumbent seeks reelection in an environment increasingly difficult for Republicans amidst the president’s plummeting popularity.
After kicking off with her criticism of his approach to the war in Iran, Collins during later exchanges pointed to her vote against Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and her opposition to the tariffs on Canada. Her debate performance was the latest example of how vulnerable Republicans are defying Trump ahead of the midterms.
When discussing the Iran war, Collins quickly called Trump out for not having a plan, and stressed how once the conflict surpassed 60 days, she voted against the war effort.
“I voted with the Democrats to bring the war to an end, but there were not sufficient votes for that to happen,” the senator said. “In addition, I agree that the president did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which part of the world’s oil travels, and I don’t feel that that was well anticipated, although it should have been.”
While Jackson sought to tie Collins to her party’s signature tax and policy bill that cut Medicaid, Collins pointed out that she ultimately did not support the bill specifically because of those cuts.
When Collins was asked about her position on Trump’s tariffs on Canada , she said, “I have been extremely outspoken in my opposition to Canadian tariffs and I have voted repeatedly to repeal them.”
But while Collins sought to highlight her distance from Trump, she also argued that she was better equipped than Jackson to work with his administration, pointing to her position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee as leverage in negotiations.
Hinson similarly sought to distance herself from Trump during her Iowa debate on two of the biggest foreign policy crises confronting the president — Russia’s war with Ukraine and the US war with Iran.
On Tuesday night she criticized Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply markets with diesel fuel in a bid to lower prices that both candidates said are hurting Iowa farmers.
“We need to lower diesel prices, but I don’t think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it,” she said.
Hinson also pointed to a 2022 congressional ban on energy imports from Russia, a measure intended to punish the Russian economy over Putin’s decision to invade Ukraine.
“I am proud to have voted for sanctions against Russia,” she said. “I’m banned from Russia because of my stance on being tough on them and supporting Ukraine, and we cannot allow Vladimir Putin to win that war.”
She also said Trump’s war with Iran “does need to come to a resolute and successful end as quickly as possible.” However, Hinson balked when asked whether she would again vote against a war powers resolution that would halt Trump’s ability to continue military action against Iran without the approval of Congress.
“I don’t think we need another resolution on the House floor. I think the president and the US military can bring it to the end,” she said.
Those breaks with Trump were notable in a debate in which Trump played a minor role — a reality owing to both Hinson’s awareness of Trump’s sagging popularity and Turek’s need to win over a share of voters who backed Trump in the 2024 election.
Hinson rarely made direct reference to Trump. But she did say she lobbied Trump personally last week to quickly get soybean trade pacts negotiated to open up foreign markets for Midwestern farmers — an acknowledgement of the economic fallout of Trump’s tariff policies.
Mike Collins spent the first Georgia Senate debate largely on the defensive. But in Tuesday’s debate, he came out swinging.
“This is a race between Georgia and Georgetown,” Collins said at the top of his opening state.
From there, Collins called Ossoff a “globetrotting trust-fund kid,” and a “coward” who hides behind “scripted online clips.” And days after Ossoff opened their last debate by telling Georgians he would put Collins’ record on trial, the Republican said it was his turn to expose his opponent’s past.
“Tough questions are going to come out tonight,” Collins said. “No one’s ever challenged Jon Ossoff on anything he’s ever voted on.”
Collins, who faces an uphill climb to knock off the incumbent Democrat, spent much of the next hour criticizing Ossoff over his record on immigration, his support for green energy initiatives and the help he’s received from LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman. He accused Ossoff of being an inadequate ally of Israel and of ignoring the interests of Georgians while he built a national profile that has fueled speculation about a future White House bid.
“He’s using us as a platform,” Collins said in his closing remarks. “Georgians are hardworking people, and we deserve a senator that will work as hard as us for us.”
For his part, Ossoff picked up where he left off at last week’s debate. He confronted Collins over his White nationalist son-in-law , criticized his support for Trump’s tariffs and tied him to the unpopular conflict with Iran. He also repeatedly pressed Collins to testify in a House ethics investigation into whether his office misused taxpayer funds.
Collins called the investigation a “political hit job” when asked. Ossoff contended he was dodging.
A testy back-and-forth in the Georgia Senate debate over files related to Jeffrey Epstein illustrated how the late financier’s crimes continue to roil American politics.
During the debate, Mike Collins attacked Ossoff over the donations he’s received from Hoffman — “the same guy that’s in the Epstein files.”
(After the Justice Department’s Epstein files showed several messages between Hoffman and Epstein, the prolific Democratic donor acknowledged he had multiple meetings with the disgraced financier. “I only knew Jeffrey Epstein because of a fundraising relationship with MIT, which I very much regret,” Hoffman wrote on X .)
“The Epstein class is on stage right now, and it’s you,” Collins said, pressing Ossoff to denounce Hoffman.
Ossoff shot back that Collins was against making the Epstein files public, a reference to a July 2025 House vote that blocked a measure that would have required the Department of Justice to release the records in 30 days. articles.title_orig: Iran shifting tactics to step up attacks on shipping before US vote, officials say
articles.title_zh: Iran shifting tactics to step up attacks on shipping before US vote, officials say
articles.content_orig:
Iran said Wednesday that a cargo ship has sunk after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, with few immediate details.
Meanwhile, a hospital in Gaza said that an Israeli strike has killed a woman. And Iran has executed a man accused of an “armed operation” against the theocracy in support of exiled former Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Wednesday. Read our full coverage here .
A cargo ship has sunk after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said. It was the first time Iran has reported a ship sinking after hitting a mine during the war.
There were few details, including about the fate of the crew. State TV quoted a Guard statement saying the ship was traveling on what it called an illegal and dangerous route when it hit the mine Wednesday morning.
It said the ship was carrying 2,500 containers when it first caught fire. The broadcaster aired images of the ship tilting into the water with a thick plume of smoke rising. The ship’s identity was not clear.
Iran has repeatedly warned ships against trying to transit the strait without its approval. The U.S. military has been guiding ships through the strait on a route off Oman on the far side.
There was no immediate verification of the sinking and no report by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations monitor.
An Israeli strike on an apartment in Gaza City killed one woman early Wednesday, according to officials at Shifa hospital.
Israel’s military said it struck a Hamas fighter but was still assessing the strike’s outcome, without elaborating.
Just over a year since a fragile ceasefire between Israel and Hamas went into effect, Israel still launches near-daily deadly strikes on the Palestinian enclave.
More than 1,490 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the ceasefire, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. Its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn’t give a breakdown of civilians and combatants, but says most of the dead are women and children.
Iran on Wednesday hanged a man accused of an “armed operation” against the theocracy in support of Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s last shah.
A report by Mizan, an outlet affiliated with the Islamic Republic’s judiciary, identified the man as Ali Sina Mostafavi and said he opened fire earlier during the Iran war and injured several people including a child in the southeastern city of Kerman.
Executions of people on similar charges have prompted an international outcry. U.N. experts this month called on Iran to halt all executions.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.
